There is a serious shortage of educational facilities for the Indians. The Indian's means of earning a livelihood are far too inadequate. Much needs to be done in regard to that. The housing situation for the Indians is almost intolerable and their health conditions are simply deplorable. There is widespread unhappiness among the Indians because of the fact that many of the treaty obligations into which this government entered with them have not been observed; in fact, they have been broken.
I am speaking only in a broad and general way in order to avoid taking up an undue amount of our time, but I think what I have said is serious enough. I would urge the government that before this parliament meets again they have a programme which will really come to grips with the problem of the Indians and deal with it. As I recall it, our committee last year recommended that the old age pension be given to the Indians. Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 449, to provide for the alteration of His Majesty's royal style and titles.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to rise to a point of order in connection with this bill. It appears in the Votes and Proceedings today and it also appears on the order paper. If the Prime Minister wants the unanimous consent of the house, we are quite happy to give it; but unless that is done this procedure is irregular.
I am opposed to this change in the King's title, for the reasons I gave last Friday, Hansard, pages 5093-94. It will lead to civil war.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I say I was surprised myself when I saw this bill on the order paper this morning. I had given the notice of the bill to be placed on the Votes and Proceedings yesterday afternoon. If the house will give its unanimous consent to introduce the bill now, I would be pleased, and I think there is everything to be gained and nothing to lose by having the measure introduced at once. May I take it that I have the leave of the house to introduce the bill?
Some lion. MEMBERS: Agreed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Hon. members will recall that in enumerating the measures which would be considered before the end of the session I was careful to say that some measures might come up of which I had no knowledge at the time I was referring to the remaining list of bills that would be brought in. This is a case in point. The request for the measure which I am now introducing came from the British government at the beginning of this week; I had no knowledge of any probability of this measure being introduced this session until I received the communication from his majesty's government in England with respect to what they hoped might take place before this session of parliament prorogued. For that reason I shall give the house immediately a more lengthy explanation in introducing the bill than otherwise might be necessary. The purpose of the bill is simply to delete the words "Indiae Imperator" and "Emperor of India" from the style and title of his majesty, but so that hon. members may see the significance of this proposal and also the necessity for it I will give the house some details as to the circumstances which have rendered it advisable to enact this pro' posal at this time.
t'Mr. Blackmore.l
Last week the United Kingdom government introduced in the House of Commons at Westminster the India independence bill. This bill provides for the setting up in India of two independent members of the commonwealth, India and Pakistan. It will take effect on August 15. Full legislative power is conferred by this bill on the legislature of each of these countries and provisions comparable to those of the Statute of Westminster are applied to them.
When this bill becomes effective the relation of His Majesty to India and Pakistan will be the same as his relation to the other fully self-governing nations of the commonwealth. It follows from this .that the title "Emperor of India" which was added to the royal style and titles in 1877 will not be appropriate.	_	_
There has been included in the India independence bill a clause declaring that the parliament of the United Kingdom assents to the omission from the royal style and titles of the words "Indiae Imperator" and "Emperor of India."
In accordance with the recitals set out in the preamble of the Statute of Westminster the consent of each parliament in the commonwealth is necessary for an alteration in the royal style and titles. The purpose of the legislation which I am introducing is to give the assent of the Canadian parliament to the deletion of the words in question.
The matter of the general revision of the royal style and titles, raised earlier in this house, is not raised either by this bill or by the bill introduced in the house at Westminster. It is to be expected that this matter will be discussed at the next meeting of commonwealth prime ministers.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 443, to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act.
He said: The purpose of this bill is to provide an allowance of §7,000 to the leader of the government in the Senate, and an allowance of §4,000 to the leader of the opposition in the Senate, in addition to the regular allowance made as sessional indemnity. May I say at once, as was mentioned yesterday by t'he hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that this measure should be considered apart altogether from the personalities involved at the moment as leaders of the government and of the opposition in the Senate respectively. All hon. members will appreciate what was said yesterday by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to the effect that both leaders in the Senate are held in the highest regard and esteem by members not only of their own house but of this house as well.	,
The question to be considered at the moment is the particular question of whether a certain allowance should be made for the leader of the government in the other house and also for the leader of the opposition in the other house. So far as the principle of the measure is concerned, it has already met with acceptance in this house. I refer to the principle of giving to the leader of the opposition an additional allowance by statute for his service as leader of the opposition. The leader of the government, of course, receives a larger remuneration than ministers of the crown generally. That may be taken in part as a recognition of the duties which he has to perform as leader of the house as well as Prime Minister.
May I say a word first of the duties of the leader of the government in the other house. In most of the parliaments of the British commonwealth, the leader of the second chamber or upper chamber, whatever it may be called, is usually a member of the government who receives the salary of a minister of the crown. For example, in the United Kingdom, Lord Addison is a member of the House of Lords. He is also the Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations, and he receives the salary which goes with that important government position. In Australia, New Zealand and in South Africa I think the arrangement is often similar, that the leader of the upper house is a minister holding a portfolio in the government and receiving the larger salary which goes with the portfolio he holds. So far as the leaders of the opposition are concerned in other parliaments of the commonwealth, I think Australia is the only country which has made provision for the leader of the opposition in the upper house. I understand that a bill has just gone through making provision for the leader of the opposition in the upper house.
May I point out that both the positions are of great responsibility. They are on the side of the house to which they relate, the most responsible positions in the two houses, because the leaders have to do with carrying on the business of the house and their office efficiently and effectively. The purpose of this measure is solely that of enabling them to perform this public function and duty more effectively and efficiently than might otherwise be possible.
The present leader of the government in the Senate is a member of the government without portfolio. He has to give to his duties an amount of his time much greater than that of any other senator.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ADDITIONAL ALLOWANCE TO GOVERNMENT AND OPPOSITION LEADERS IN SENATE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADDITIONAL ALLOWANCE TO GOVERNMENT AND OPPOSITION LEADERS IN SENATE
speechtext:
My hon. friend says "hear, hear." I think everyone will agree with that. He has to give a greater amount of time to the business of the country than any other member of the Senate would be expected to give. In order to perform that duty efficiently the leader of the government in the Senate has to be familiar with the government's policy and programme in all particulars. To be familiar with the government's policy and programme he has to attend meetings of cabinet very regularly. He has to attend those meetings not only during the time when the Senate is in session but between sessions as well. If hon. members opposite ever come to have the experience of preparing a parliamentary programme they will realize that it involves a good deal of time and thought on the part of ministers, whether with or without portfolio, for some little time before parliament meets. That is but one of the official duties. I need not say to hon. members today how much more complicated the business of legislation is at this time than it has ever been heretofore. The best evidence of that is the length of the parliamentary sessions themselves. If parliaments held sessions of two, three, or

four months it might be expected that leaders might be found to take on these extra obligations without expecting to be in any way recompensed financially for that obligation; however when a parliamentary sessions lasts, as ours apparently are going to continue to last, and as they have been in the last few years, for half a year or more, it is imposing a very heavy obligation on any individual, both financially and otherwise, to expect him to be able to familiarize himself with the legislation that comes before the two houses in the course of a particular session, and to explain policy as well as particulars of legislation. The character of the legislation, as I have indicated, is much more intricate and comprehensive in every way than has been the case with legislation in the past.
This house is familiar with the amount of time that has been given this session to international questions. The Senate is perhaps in many ways in a better position to devote a great deal of its time to international problems than is this house. Every encouragement should be given to the members of the upper house to give a. great deal of time and attention to all-important world problems. The leader of the government and the leader of the opposition in the Senate have to familiarize themselves with these problems. If they are to do that they will have to give a great deal of extra time to that particular work. There are also the individual measures that come from this house. The leader of the government has to make arrangements with members of his following, no matter in which house it is, to take charge of particular measures as they come up. To do that he himself has to be more or less familiar with the measures that are being brought forward. As I say, all of these things make the office of leader of .the government in the other house a much more responsible one today than it has been at any previous time.
Here I think I might as well answer the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre at once about the strengthening of the Senate. He said yesterday he was surprised that a Liberal government, which has aimed at reforming the Senate, should bring in a measure of this kind. The responsibility of the leader in the Senate is very great. As I was about to say when I was interrupted, hon. members are talking about not enough business being done in the Senate, about not enough bills coming from the Senate to this house. I say that that is largely the result of the fact that no leader, under the financial obligations which he must incur at this time, can, unless he is going to be compensated in some way for the extra time he will have to give to these questions, manage effectively the business of the Senate so as to ensure measures being introduced there in the first place, debated there and brought over to this house. The provision this bill seeks to make will help both the leader of the government and the leader of the opposition to give more of their time to the introduction of legislation in the other house and to careful discussion of it before it comes over to this house.
My hon. friend said that he was surprised that a Liberal government should introduce this measure, because we stood for democracy as well as for reform of the Senate. He argued that this was not a democratic measure. May I draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that we have pretty well reached the point so far as the Senate is concerned, and indeed so far as this house is concerned as well, where, unless the leaders are wealthy men, they are not going to be able to carry on the business of leadership. A measure of this kind will make it possible for any man, whether he be a man of means or one who is not too well off, if he is a leader to devote his time to the extent that it should be devoted to public business in the other house.
I attach a great deal of importance to that because I think one of the great reforms that has been made through the years has been that of recognizing that even members of parliament, who may not have any special obligations, have a right to expect a certain indemnity. But you cannot expect a person receiving only the ordinary indemnity, especially with taxation as it has come to be, to give as much time as he would like to be able to give, if he wishes to do his work effectively, in the position of leadership, with all that that involves ai this time. So I

Senate and House oj Commons Act
say to my hon. friend that this is a reform in that it will enable the Senate to function more effectively than it has up to the present, if on that score there is any exception to be taken. It will enable the leaders to organize the business of the upper house in a more effective way, and to that extent it will be assisting public business generally.
My hon. friend went on to say that the Senate was a useless institution. I think that was the phrase he used, or something to that effect. May I say that we are not debating the question at the moment whether the second house should be abolished, but I should be very surprised indeed if the people of Canada generally would not perhaps feel a greater need than ever for a second house if the C.C.F. - ever got into power. I can assure them that they need have no anxiety over the attitude of the public toward this measure. If my hon. friends were in power the public would need no end of safeguards-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADDITIONAL ALLOWANCE TO GOVERNMENT AND OPPOSITION LEADERS IN SENATE
speechtext:
The point I wish to make is this: so far as the other house
is concerned, if one takes its complexion it is impossible to say that it is representative of the vested interests or the big interests, or is made up of wealthy men. When one has regard for the positions which those hon. members held in public life, whether they were appointed by this government or by previous governments, he will realize that in most cases the appointments to the Senate were made from members of this House of Commons, from those who had had great experience or extra experience as ministers of the crown, or long experience in conducting the affairs of government. They were appointed' because the government of the day knew that they represented, the will and the wishes of the people or they would never have got into this House of Commons. I say to my hon friend that he had better not seek to reflect either upon the characteristics or the callings of hon. members of the other house of this parliament.
I have spoken of the necessity of giving the leader of the government in the other house a salary. I have said very little about the position of the leader of the opposition. I would draw the attention of the house to the fact that at one time no salary was paid to the leader of the opposition in this house. Twenty years and more ago special provision was made for the position of the leader of the opposition in this house. Why was that done? It was done as a means of furthering the public interest by assigning to one leader the special obligation of watching the progress of legislation as it went through this house and continually guarding the public interest from the point of view of the opposition as well as of the government.
So far as the positions of leader of the opposition in the Senate and in this House of Commons are concerned, the difference is in degree not in kind. The leader of the opposition in the Senate has to give a great deal of extra time to studying the measures that come before that house, in making arrangements with the leader of the government in regard to the conduct of business from day .to day, in associating himself with the work of committees, in meeting delegations and deputations. He has to meet the extra expense to which all leaders in public life are put. Unless we are going to have only wealthy men filling positions of high responsibility some additional remuneration will have to be given to the gentlemen who are in these responsible positions or else they will not be able to give as much of their time to them as otherwise would be the case.
I submit to the house that the time has come when, in the public interest and for the

Senate and House of Commons Act
more effective discharge of public business, some additional allowance should be made to both the leader of the government and the leader of the opposition in the other house. I repeat, the reasons are much the same as have governed in this house. The change in the times necessitates this as their duties grow greater and greater from day to day and from year to year. Some special provision, I submit, is imperative if we are to have public business done as the country expects it to be done in both houses of parliament.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ADDITIONAL ALLOWANCE TO GOVERNMENT AND OPPOSITION LEADERS IN SENATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the bill before us, Bill No. 443, is a bill to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said, in this bill the government proposes giving an additional allowance to the leader of the government and to the leader of the opposition in another place. In this discussion I am wandering whether one has to use that outmoded term or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADDITIONAL ALLOWANCE TO GOVERNMENT AND OPPOSITION LEADERS IN SENATE
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ADDITIONAL ALLOWANCE TO GOVERNMENT AND OPPOSITION LEADERS IN SENATE
speechtext:
I think it is time we got back to straight, talk and spoke of this institution respectfully as what it is, the Senate of Canada.
The bringing forward of this bill indicates that the government feels that the position of both leaders in the Senate carries with it greater responsibilities, and on this ground they base the present proposal of giving them an additional allowance. As to greater responsibilities, I am sure there can be no question about that. The question that does arise is one of curiosity: Why, if greater responsibilities justify an increase to the men who now hold these positions, has an additional allowance not been given prior to this time? This government has been in office for twenty years or so, but has never before made any move in this direction. We have had confederation for eighty years, and no move has been made in this direction. The Prime Minister has indicated that at the moment greater responsibilities devolve upon us all. That is true. Yet the fact remains that in all these past years the men who occupy these positions in the Senate did carry greater responsibilities than their associates who were private members in that house.
In view of the statement which the Prime Minister has made and the statement made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) the other day I think perhaps I should take a moment to explain oui position with reference to this measure. It can be briefly stated.

If the leaders in the other house have added responsibilities I think there is every justification for giving consideration to a larger allowance for them. How much that should be may be a matter of judgment. The government in its wisdom has indicated that the leader of the government in the Senate should get an additional allowance of $7,000 and the leader of the opposition an additional allowance of $4,000, making a total allowance to the leader of the government there of $13,000 and a total for the leader of the opposition of $10,000. I think on the basis of added responsibilities there is something to be said for making these greater allowances. If the Senate is an essential part of our government institutions we cannot just pass off a measure like this without giving it some reasonable consideration. On the other hand if that institution does require some reform and has not had it, and there is no proposal here that measures shall be taken to bring about reforms in the Senate that would be in the public welfare, there is some excuse for saying, as a measure of protest, that we do not want to take a position of supporting this institution in its present form by this action. I say there may be some justification for that.
As to greater responsibilities there can be no question. As to the essential place which this institution occupies in our government there can be no question. The only question is whether steps should not be taken for its reform.
Our position is briefly this: We believe in a second chamber. We do not believe in the abolition of the Senate. We do believe in its reform. We believe in maintaining that institution for several reasons, as a check against hasty and ill-considered legislation, as a protection for minorities, as a protection for the provinces in a federal system, and there may be other reasons. As I said, we are opposed to the abolition of the Senate. But we do think it should be reformed. I make no comment now on the various suggestions which have been made as to how it should be reformed. Some have said that its members should be elected by the people and not be appointed by a party government.

One suggestion that has been made is that the members of the Senate

Senate and House of Commons Act
should be elected by the people rather than appointed by a party government. Another suggestion is that their term of office should be fixed, some have said at ten years, others for different terms, rather than that it should be a life appointment. Some have said that the provincial governments should be allowed in some way or other to choose some of the members of the Senate, and some have suggested that they should choose half of its membership. Some have said that the present incumbents in the Senate should not be disturbed. I am in some sympathy with each one of these proposals, but I make no comment on them now.
My suggestion is this, that there should be called together a joint committee, a representative body composed of representatives of this house and from the other place and representatives from the provinces, to consider the situation as it now exists in our parliamentary system and see what can be done to strengthen the Senate, having in mind nothing else but the welfare of the Canadian people. That is my proposal. That is our position, andi in that position I have the support of some outstanding men in Canada. I want to read what one of them had to say at a time when he was a crusader for Senate reform and other kinds of reform. I am glad to know that at one time he supported the policy we now stand for. I am quoting from a paper which at that time was a strong supporter of the present government, known then as the Globe. This is from its issue of Monday, September 7, 1925. when the party opposite had a crusading spirit and progressive policies and when some of its members supported what I now advocate, and I hope when I sit down they will all support my proposal. This is what that great Liberal newspaper had to say, referring to the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King):
No declaration by the Prime Minister throughout the whole of his address was more enthusiastically received by the North York electors than that in which he declared for Senate reform. Loud "hear, hear" and applause which lasted nearly two minutes greeted his declaration:	"We believe one of the great necessities
of the time is Senate reform."
We have had this morning one evidence of his notion of senate reform. I do not know what others there have been in the intervening 21 or 22 years, but we have had one evidence this morning. The report goes on:
But the difficulty in consummating Senate reform, Premier King proceeded, lay in the fact that the Senate itself had to approve of any parliamentary measure to reform it, and its members could not be removed by any action of the people or the commons.
"Who appoints them?" demanded a member of the audience. "I am coming to that", replied the premier.
"Throw them put", demanded several other's in chorus.
Then the report continues:
Proposed interprovincial conferences to discuss Senate reform, went on Mr. King, constitute at best an attempt to reform the Senate from without, whereas reform from within was the only effective way in which it could be brought about. He proposed reforming it from within by appointing hereafter only men pledged to oarry out the policies of the Liberal government.
Now in so far as that particular reform is concerned, the Prime Minister has carried it out.

speechtext:
I presume all the senators who have been appointed since that time have signed on the dotted line this requirement by the Prime Minister so that he can now have any kind of Senate reform that is desirable. I think that is a good position to have them in, but I would like to be assured by the Prime Minister that he has that assurance from them all, and I would like to have that verified by them all.
Now what is the situation, Mr. Speaker? Here is a body which is necessary to our form of government. It is filled by appointments from the parties that are in power. One party is in power a long time and gets many of its supporters there. At the present time there are 66 supporting the government and 22 against them, appointed on the regional basis. I believe there are 24 from the maritimes, 24 from each of the central provinces and 24 from the west. But it has resulted in a onesided representation over there; it has resulted in failure to get anything like occupational representation.
I am the last to suggest that that should be the basis of representation in any parliamentary body, but at least there should be some approach to better occupational representation than there is today, because in that body, out of 96 members there are only

13-who can be classed as farmers and only one who can be called a labour man.
Our position, briefly, is this. Some justification can. be made for paying men for additional work they do. We can approach this thing from the point of view of prejudice and say, "Well, there is popular prejudice against this institution and we will not do anything to help it". I do not think that is a constructive approach. We can approach it from another point of view also, and say, "We have done little for old age, the aged people in this country, giving them an increase of only SCO a year, and here we are going to give seven thousand to one man and so much to another.
I suggest that is not the statesmanlike approach to the matter. We are prepared to support the government in this measure provided they will give us some assurance that some steps along these lines will be taken to try to lay the foundation for reforming this institution so as to make it more useful for the people of Canada. If the government can give us that assurance we will support them in this measure eveu though at the moment it may not be the popular thing to do. If they cannot give us that assurance they must proceed with their measure without our support.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ADDITIONAL ALLOWANCE TO GOVERNMENT AND OPPOSITION LEADERS IN SENATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in just a sentence I should like to repeat the remark I made yesterday, that we approach this matter on its merits with regard to the principle at stake and not with reference to any personalities at all. I am grateful 'to the Prime Minister for echoing the sentiments I expressed yesterday with regard to the two men who would be immediately affected. I would like to go one step further and say that not only have I a high regard for the two men immediately affected, but I have had the privilege of meeting and getting to know a number of other senators, and I regard them as men who have rendered a distinguished public service, men to be held in high esteem. We are all agreed on that phase of the matter and on the fact that we are discussing this as a matter of principle.
I also wish to point out that the amount of money involved in this bill is, in terms of federal budgets, infinitesimal. The total amount of money to be added to the cost of government by this bill is only SI 1,000 a year. When one takes time to debate such a measure it is because a principle is at stake. I want to say that I agree with *those who have said that work should be paid for. But I am not yet convinced that Their Honours in the other place are underpaid for the amount of

Senate and House of Commons Act
work which is given them to do. As for the suggestion of the Prime Minister that they should be given more work and that we start paying their leaders first in order to encourage them to take on more work, I submit that is contrary to the democratic approach and contrary to the whole aim at Senate reform which was in the crusading heart of the Prime Minister over twenty years ago. I. know that during recent years from some quarters of this house there have been requests for more work to originate in the Senate, but they have not come from this group. We fee'l, as the Prime Minister felt twenty years ago, that the elected representatives of the people should have supremacy in matters of legislation. The Prime Minister's whole case for paying this extra money rests upon the assumption that the place of the Senate in our parliament set-up is a justifiable one.
I am not going into the arguments for abolition of the Senate at this time, because we who favour that course are in a minority in this house. But I feel, as the leader of the opposition didi, that we have a right and duty to appeal to hon. members opposite- to measure up, as the Prime Minister put it, to their own high ideals and purposes. I do not deny for one minute that hon. members opposite are just as high in their ideals and purposes as we in this group claim to be; and I am tired of these references to righteousness on the part of members in any quarter in this house. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, as one reads the pages of Hansard in years gone by, and as one reads party platforms, he finds in Liberal literature the highest of idealism and purposes down across the years. But what bothers us is that they can hold those ideals for years and years and never do anything about them.
I observe, Mr. Speaker, that you have picked up the bill, no doubt as a suggestion that I should speak about it; and that is, in fact, what I propose to do. The bill before us is No. 443, an act to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act, to provide what the Prime Minister implies today is reform of the Senate. The Prime Minister used that very expression; he said he thought this was a reform which was long overdue. I cannot see that it is in any sense an expression of the kind of reform of the Senate for which the Liberal party has stood down across the years. I want to say something about the position of the Liberal party, as did the leader of the opposition. But before I do so, there are two other remarks of the Prime Minister to which I wish to make a brief answer.
First of all, I wish to point out to the Prime Minister that in my remarks yesterday I did not refer to individuals in the Senate as representing vested interests. What I said was that we were creating a vested interest in the Senate itself, by strengthening it in this way. The other point I wish to make in reply to what the Prime Minister said is to the effect that I think he let the cat out of the bag when he said that when the C.C.F. comes to power it might, in his opinion, be good for Canada still to have the Senate there. The implication there was that, after the people of Canada have decided in a democratic way that they want the C.C.F. in power, a Senate appointed by the Liberals, appointed largely by the Prime Minister himself, should, he thinks, still be there to block legislation which the people of this country had declared they wanted by putting this party in power. That is a far cry from the position the Prime Minister took in this House of Commons on July 19, 1924, which was a position similar to the one he took on a number of occasions during those early twenties when the majority in the Senate was against him. In that period of time, with his crusading spirit, he rose in this house time and time again and declared that this House of Commons should be supreme, that this House of Commons should have the right to enact the legislation which it was elected by the people of Canada to put on the statute books.
On July 19, 1924, the Senate had, by a certain device, rejected proposed amendments made by the House of Commons to the Pension Act, the act having to do with military pensions. The House of Commons was put in a jam; they had to accept the deletions made in the other place in order not to lose some of the benefits that were in the amendments to the Pension Act which had been passed by this house. After the house had faced the fact that it was in a jam and had to agree to it, the Prime Minister had this to say. as reported in Hansard of July 19, 1924, at page 4S72:
Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King (Prime Minister):	Mr. Speaker, having in mind the
action of the second chamber with respect to the measure which has just been amended and also the fate of a number of bills adopted by the Commons and defeated in the Senate. I think hon. members will agree with me that the time has come when the Commons in Canada should seek to gain rights and privileges with respect to legislation originating in this chamber similar to those which have obtained by the House of Commons in the parliament at Westminster. I may say that the government had under consideration, prior to the opening of this session, legislation with this end in view, but we were anxious the public should feel fully convinced of the necessity before pressing it on the attention of parliament.

Senate and House oj Commons Act
Later in, that same statement-and remember that this is back in 1924, twenty-three years ago-he said:
I desire to assure the house that when parliament reassembles steps will be taken by the government to obtain, if possible, means whereby bills may be enacted by and with the advice and consent of the House of Commons under conditions similar in principle to those which have been sanctioned for the parliament of the United Kingdom.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if the principle that the Commons should be supreme was sound back in 1924, the Prime Minister should not alter that principle when he envisages the possibility of the C.C.F. being .in power.

I want to point out that this is exactly what it does; it crystallizes the Senate in its present form. I found it a bit difficult to follow the position taken by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), but I think I got it before he finished. I take it that he is not prepared to agree to this measure unless he gets an assurance from the Prime Minister that the Senate will be reformed somewhat along the lines he suggested. In view of the fact that these promises to reform the Senate have been

The assurance that it will be done puts it on a pretty long-range basis, from our experience with the Prime Minister. I think it is going about it the wrong way to say yes, we will agree to this now, but we do so on the understanding that next year or the year after you will bring in some Senate reforms. I think the leader of the opposition would be better advised to say to the Prime Minister-and I am talking on their terms, not ours-"We will oppose this measure until you bring it in as part of an over-all reform of the Senate."

I find that Sir Wilfrid Laurier introduced a bill to amend the act respecting the Senate and House of Commons on April 20, 1905, and section 2 of that bill reads:

It is like the Senate itself; it has taken a long time to reform it, but there has been a tremendous reformation.
My hon. friends have read quotations of mine about democratic legislation having been thrown out whenever it went over to the other house. That was the condition when we came into office. There was very little chance in those days of getting through both houses measures of the type of social legislation we have since put through because it would be turned down in the other house. But what a change has taken place since that time. I promised that we would see that the Senate was reformed so that liberal measures that were being enacted would be put through. May I say that we have carried out that reform much more thoroughly and effectively than I ever believed would be possible at the time I made that statement. If we stay here much longer you may be sure that that reform will go on, and we will make doubly sure that democratic measures and social legislation passed by this house will get through the upper house.
I should like to correct one impression some hon. members appear to have. Apparently it is thought that the leader of the government in the Senate, as a cabinet minister without portfolio, receives a salary. May I say that he gets nothing at all as a. minister without portfolio either in the way of salary or allowance. Being a member of the government and having to have a knowledge of government business, its programme, policy and the like, the leader of the government in the Senate is obliged to have a residence in this city practically the whole year round, and he is put to that additional expense.
These are things which I think it is only right should be known to hon. members. The provision being made by this bill is something that will govern through the years to come. Before I conclude, may I say this to my friends of the C.C.F. who suggest that Liberals in the Senate might be inclined to throw out some of their legislation should they come to power. If I am correctly informed, the president of the C.C.F. party in British Columbia made this statement:
The first duty of this party when it comes to power is the bold and ruthless removal from private hands of the means of production.

If there is anything like that, I can tell my hon. friends that it certainly will be thrown out by the Senate. Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at one o'clock we were discussing Bill 443, an act to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act, and I had only nicely started my introduction. The bill proposes to increase the present allowances to the leader of the government and the leader of the opposition in the Senate. My first reaction is something like this. Of course, I am a social crediter, and my social credit conscience seems never to permit me to vote against giving something to somebody, especially when that person or those people contribute something to the country's welfare.
Even though I have sometimes perhaps_ expressed myself on increases in judges' salaries and increases in the salaries of those engaged in the diplomatic service, I always feel a little guilty if I oppose them, because it is only increasing the benefits to the individual, and why should I not want to increase the benefits accruing to people? But of course a principle is involved. While I am a social crediter I am not living in a social credit country. I am living in a country controlled by a party that believes in a policy which will not permit of my social credit instincts functioning. Therefore it boils down to this, that living as I am in this country, apparently to vote to give someone an additional financial benefit means in the net result voting to take something away from somebody else. That is the position in which I find myself.
I can quite understand, perhaps, my friends to my immediate right being so enthusiastic about their position in respect to this bill, because, as I understand that socialist philosophy, it is that in order that benefits may accrue to the substratum of society it is necessary to reduce the benefits from those who have more than others. I do not believe that has to be done; it would not if the country were handled properly. In other words, I do not believe that you have to tear the fop fellow down in order to build up the fellow who is underneath. That is a wrong philosophy, it is a wrong mental attitude to take, and anyone who looks at a bill like this and says, "Well now, here these people in the other place, who are getting the same as we are getting, $6,000 a year, are to have another addition, which wall mean that one will get $13,000 a year and the other less, and perhaps some other additions-well, I cannot stand for that; he is getting too much"; to such a person, I say, that mental attitude is wrong.
[Mr. Hansell.)
To my mind nobody gets too much provided he is not taking it from somebody else. There is my position. I am dealing now with a mental attitude, and I would like the house to think that through some time, particularly when members are suffering from insomnia and want something to think about.
As to what has been said about abolishing the Senate, I must confess that with my present knowledge of the entire parliamentary set-up, plus the history of parliamentary institutions, I personally would not be so bold as to say at the present time that I want the Senate abolished, that they are no good- what is the use of them. You hear that sort of talk, and I am inclined to think that underlying that attitude is another principle, and that is the desire that I must not be checked in what I am going to do. That too is a mental attitude. I do not know whether it would be the best thing for a government to be elected and have an absolutely free hand, without any check whatsoever, to do whatever they thought best on the spur of the moment. I can visualize a danger there. Governments are not always right, and if the Senate of Canada were what I think it should be, they would have an excellent opportunity of checking something that governments might do which in the end would be wrong.
I do not want to bring in my friends to my immediate right, but they were wrong in their attitude towards the war when the war broke out. There is no question that time proved they were wrong, just as wrong as anyone could ever be. Of course that was on a negative proposition; they did not want something done that was about to be done. But suppose they were in office and desired a positive thing that was just as wrong; I do not know why a properly functioning body in the other place would not be a good thing.
I am perhaps thinking out loud now when I mention those particular things. I can visualize, under this party system, a government being elected on a tremendous emotional appeal at a time when people's hearts and minds were tremendously confused and the country was being saddled with an irresponsible government. I am not now referring to my hon. friends opposite. They may or may not be. I do not care about that. I am visualizing a situation which might easily arise, where the country is confused and dissatisfied and a great emotional appeal is made to the people. They are fed up with what they have and they are taking a chance on something new, something of which perhaps they have little knowledge, and an irresponsible government is elected with no check whatever on what they do and the methods they take.

Senate and House of Commons Act
They may be well-meaning; they may have good intentions. They desire to reach a certain objective, but in trying to do so they pass legislation and devise methods of reaching their objective which might very well wreck this whole country. I say it might be as well if we had some little check through the medium of the Senate.
There is another point I should like to make here. There does seem to me to be some justification for increasing the salaries of the leader of the government and the leader of the opposition in the Senate. What I mean is this. I understand that they now receive the same remuneration as all other senators. It seems to me that their responsibilities are heavier and that they should receive something more than the other senators receive. I am not opposed to an increase. Whether the increase should be the amount provided, I am not prepared to say. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) spoke he pointed out that the leaders in the other house are under additional expense. Perhaps the government leader in the Senate has to maintain a residence in Ottawa. Those arguments are all right, and I am not opposing them; but the Prime Minister did not refer to another phase which I think is worthy of consideration, namely that under the present system all senators are appointed for life. One cannot compare them with the leader of the opposition in this house, for instance, or the Prime Minister, or any other minister, because their tenure of office may not be long. They do not know how long it will last, while the senators have economic security for the rest of their lives. That should be taken into consideration, I think, when an amount is determined.
There was another thing which struck me, and it was this. All that the Prime Minister said, even though we grant it to be true, has been true for the last thirty, forty or fifty years. I cannot quite understand why at this session the government has suddenly decided to increase the salaries of those two leaders. If they need that increase today, they needed it last year and they needed it twenty years ago. That is a point which I think is worthy of noting.
With respect to that part of the debate which has emphasized Senate reform, I have just a word or two to say. I certainly believe that we need Senate reform. I would go farther; I would say we certainly need parliamentary reform, and the Senate is part of parliament. I once said that I thought senators should be elected. I still think so, because upon their election they would be sent to the Senate to represent the will of the people.

At the present time, when they are appointed by the government in office, they naturally feel that they must be loyal to those who appointed them. But they might be loyal to those who appointed them and not loyal to the people. If they are not elected I think that at least the provinces should have something to do with the appointments. Is it not passing strange, for instance, that although there is in Alberta a government which has been known as a Social Credit government, holding a different concept from that which the present Liberal administration holds, a Social Credit government which swept out all its opponents twelve years ago and has been in office ever since, yet the Liberal government here in Ottawa has been appointing Liberal senators from that province from that day twelve years ago up to the present.

I do not think that is right. I believe some body should be set up-first I thought of a joint parliamentary committee of both houses, and then in terms of a royal commission, but somehow or other

I do not rush too quickly into suggesting it should be a royal commission-for the purpose of going into parliamentary reform, with the .[DOT]specific view of bringing about such reforms as will ensure that at all times the will of the people is reflected. That is not what happens today; positively it is not. The other day we had a bill dealing with old age pensions. Would anyone say that the means test reflects the will of the people of Canada? It does not. So I say there is need for Senate reform.
In conclusion let me say that I do not like to oppose a reasonable bill. I am not saying I oppose an increase for these two public servants who sit in the Senate. However, I think my position will have to be that of the leader of this group; that what we want is a bill embracing the over-all picture of parliamentary reform. If that is done, and something of this sort is brought in, it will meet with more favour as far as I am concerned. I shall have to take the position my leader has well taken, and oppose the bill. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a word to say in reply to my hon. friend (Mr. Irvine) who has made as usual a delightful speech. He says that the Senate does not always reflect public opinion. It is a respectable view, but I think that my hon. friend is wrong, because in the Senate there are twelve or fifteen owners of newspapers. They establish public opinion, and therefore the views of the public must be in conformity with their own.
At first I was opposed to the Senate. I said to myself, so long as Senator Dandurand and Senator Aylesworth, dear Sir Allen, are there, I will not go further with the suggestion of abolishing the Senate. But if the government has not done much that has been seen in the reform of the Senate, the senators
have taken it up themselves and they have reformed themselves to a great degree. We see that they are very active now and they show some independence. In the Senate we see some dignified old Conservatives and some Liberals who are really democrats. They unite together to make some profitable suggestions to the government,
I must say, sir, that I am honoured in counting amongst my friends some old gentlemen who sit in the Senate and who are just as worthy of sitting there as any hon. member is to sit here. The Senate has done no harm in the past, and now it is starting to do some good. The only thing is to warn the government to be very cautious about the appointment of a future leader in the Senate. The present one stated one day that the Prime Minister would lead the small nations at the peace conference, which was just flattery. It was not interesting, it was not worth listening to, and he got his place. But there are others who practise flattery in order to replace the present incumbent. I will name no one, but it is clear and evident that the practice is followed. The Prime Minister has too much experience of men not to read between the lines when something of that sort is said to him.
Even when I was opposed to the Senate because at the time they had not started their own reform I never complained bitterly about them as some of my hon. friends did today. The senators are able men who represent a good1 slice of mankind. They do not pretend that they are any better than the commoners but they live a life that is more boring when they wait for legislation that takes so much time to come from the House of Commons. They deserve our sympathy; they deserve our assistance; they deserve our help, and it is to be hoped that in the future the Senate will not be castigated by the House of Commons any more than the Senate does this house, but that there will be a spirit of cooperation between both houses. That spirit is highly desirable. It is unfortunate that at times there are closed walls between both houses. There should be more frequent communication and exchange of views between the senators and the members of the House of Commons. When that is done there will be no more complaint about- the Senate.
This bill is a trivial matter; it is just to increase by a few thousand dollars the amount that is paid to the leaders of both parties. I am not very well acquainted with the leader of the government in the Senate. I believe that he is doing a good' job in his

position; but I am well acquainted with the leader of the opposition in the Senate, who has been here for a very long time. He is a dignified old gentleman and works very hard. I remember that Senator Dandurand, although he was very old, used to wake up at four or five in the morning to start his day. As the Prime Minister said, 'he had no extra pay to lead the government in the Senate; it was quite meritorious of him to be up so early in the morning to start his day. I know some other senators who are public spirited just as much as any other member of any group in the house. They express independent views -perhaps because 'they are in the other house, I do not know; but they express independent views for the welfare of the community and on this account deserve highly from the country.

Reference has been made to pledges exacted from members going to the Senate. That was a mere understanding, a gentleman's agreement with some of those who went to the Senate at the beginning of my term of office as Prime Minister. Of late years I have not felt it was necessary to suggest this reform to any senator; I believe many already favour it.
I have always looked upon every member ' of parliament, whether he was in the Senate or in this house, as being independent in the matter of expressing his views, and I hope this measure will help to further that same independence.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: COMPENSATION TO PROVINCES IN LIEU OP INCOME AND OTHER TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this question was before the house last evening the Minister of Finance was good enough to allow the adjournment of the debate in order that I and others might have an opportunity of examining certain documents he asked to be placed on Hansard and which had not been seen. I am sure that all hon. members of the house have since seen those documents. The minister was good enough to let me have them last night.. I have looked them over. They have to do only with the formulae for arriving at the amounts of money to be paid to the various provinces under varying conditions. I think they contain nothing more fundamental than that. As far as that point goes, the documents which the minister tabled I think added nothing new, except in detail, to the facts he presented last night and to other facts he had presented at other times. Since last night I have also had the opportunity of looking over the minister's remarks, and I think I can conclude my observations with respect to them in a very short time.
What the minister had to say only confirms our worst doubts and fears. He simply repaints the dismal picture of this government's calculated objective to get from the provinces certain taxation rights by any means and at any cost. The minister also made it plain that

Tax Agreements with Provinces
the government is going to back away from its 1945 proposals because they are more burdensome than it can afford. In that respect the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) a few days ago also gave us notice that he expects the provinces to assume a greater share of the cost of old age pensions. With respect to public investment, public works, unemployment and so on, those plans which were aimed not only at a greater measure of social security but also at lessening the prospect of a recession, there is nothing proposed. The minister makes it clear with respect to the minor taxes that while the government will bargain with respect to them, the dominion will abandon nothing. If all these things had been considered in a conference and an agreement had been achieved, the story would have been different and the effect would have been different. But this method of playing one province off against another, and playing some provinces off against others, is to be deplored. For that kind of procedure the government is deserving of the severest censure.
The question now is, what are we going to do about the bill? What is this bill? This bill is simply enabling legislation. Apparently seven provinces have assured the government that they are prepared to accept the government's plan. As I understand it, no agreements are signed. This is therefore an enabling bill to give the government power to enter arrangements with the provinces by which the provinces will give up the right to collect certain taxes and in return the government will make certain payments to the provinces. In that respect we do not intend to take the position that this agreement made between the government and several other governments cannot be signed. We therefore shall not vote against this bill. But we want it made clear that certain of the results of the method which the government has followed are objectionable, not only to us but, we think, objectionable to most Canadians.
Last night I stated my objections to the government's whole programme. It is now clear that the government has abandoned its social security, health and unemployment proposals as announced two years ago. Its policy does not embody in any real sense the principle of fiscal need. If the principle of fiscal need is in it, it is only incidental in this arrangement by which the government is proposing to extract from the taxpayers of this country a great deal of money and hand it over to the provinces to spend. It is virtually buying the provinces out of their taxation
rights, and doing it with the money that the government is going to subtract from its own plans for social security, health and so-called public investment, as proposed two years ago. That is made clear by the minister's own statements here and elsewhere, which I shall put on the record in a moment. I am sure he will not object, because he repeated last night statements which he had made previously. He stated that to the extent these offers to the provinces are generous, to that extent will the provinces have to assume greater responsibility and to that extent will the dominion government do less in the way of carrying out its proposals of two years ago.
By way of summary, let me say this with respect to the criticisms I offered last night. I said the government's proposal goes a long way to promoting disunity. That must be apparent to anyone who reads the minister's address of yesterday. On page 7 of the typewritten address he let me have-and it is at page 5310 of Hansard-he put on the record the minimum amounts which would go to the different provinces in Canada if this scheme goes through, and the maximum amounts that might go to them on the basis of the year 1947. In the one case the amount is $206,000,000 odd; and in the other case it is $228,000,000 odd. When one looks at those figures he sees that the minimum amount that is going to the provinces, if the w'hole nine of them went into it, would be $206,000,000, and the amount going to the seven provinces which have indicated their willingness to sign is $83,000,000. I suppose two-thirds of that will be collected from the taxpayers of Ontario and Quebec, which provinces have not signed and are therefore left out of this arrangement. The province of Quebec was to receive $56,000,000 odd and the province of Ontario $67,000,000 odd, in minimum amounts, a total of about $123,000,000. So as a result of the government's policies we have seven provinces getting $83,000,000, two-thirds of which is collected from outside their boundaries, and the two provinces in which that two-thirds is collected getting nothing; In that there is not only cause for disunity, but we must also keep in mind that if this government does not pay the money to Ontario and Quebec, or if those provinces do not accept it, the taxpayers of Canada will have that much less to pay, and the budgetary problems of this government will be made that much easier.
I want to examine now the other table of payments that are based on the 1947 figures. This shows the total cost to be $228,000,000, with seven provinces getting $91,000,000 odd,

of which, as I say, two-thirds or more would be collected outside those provinces. The remaining two provinces would receive $137,000,000, in the case of Quebec $63,000,000 and in the case of Ontario $74,000,000, with the taxpayers of those two provinces being taxed to pay two-thirds of the money going to the other seven provinces while themselves getting nothing. My point there is that this method, whatever merit it may have, at least leads to disunity.
My second point is that in a federal state a procedure of this kind goes a long way toward centralizing the taxing power in one government. To the extent we go in that direction, to that extent we are leading to a unitary state; and to the extent that we become a unitary state we are simply saying good-bye to confederation as we have known it in this country.
My third point is that in a federal state the plan now before us fails to give the province any clear fieild of taxation. In that connection I want to read a brief statement from page 85 of book 2 of the report of the Rowe'll-Sirois commission, a report which I regard very highly and to which the minister paid a high compliment last evening. Dealing with the proposals brought forward which aimed to leave with the provinces certain of the minor fields of taxation, the report says:
It is implicit in the plan, but should be clearly stated, that the dominion will respect the tax fields left to the provinces. Adjustments in the joint dominion-provineial-municipal tax structure will undoubtedly be necessary and desirable from time to time. But the dominion can no longer consider itself a free and independent agent to take unilateral action to this end when it pleases. The essence of the plan is to leave provinces and municipalities with adequate, stable revenues, and this would clearly be defeated if the dominion should extend its taxation into fields already occupied by the provinces or on objects jointly taxed without making satisfactory compensatory adjustments. Such action would violate the whole spirit of the arrangement.
That was their statement with respect to minor taxes under their proposed settlement.
The fourth criticism I offered of this plan was that it has failed to achieve a continuance of plans for dominion-provincial discussions, which in my view is a serious matter in a federal state. Here it is important that we go to great lengths to try and get the maximum of cooperation between the central government and the other governments across the dominion. In my judgment the course the government is following will lead to the liquidation of the dominion-provincial conference system which has 'been inherent in our set-up since the first years of confederation.

My fifth criticism was that this procedure delays the bringing into effect of the social security, health, unemployment and other plans envisaged in what was spoken of two years ago as a great national plan. In that connection I want to read a statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) himself, and then to refer to his own words in dosing his address last evening. Addressing the Toronto board of trade on January 27 of this year the Minister of Finance had this to say:
As a result of increased rental payments from the dominion-
That was after the dominion had proposed to increase its rental payments above the figures proposed in some earlier discussions.
-the provinces will be able to assume, and must expect to assume, a somewhat greater financial responsibility.
I commend the minister for his frankness. The dominion offered to give the provinces more, but to the extent that it gave them more it would do less itself. That should be clear to anyone examining the matter, but when we have the statement so frankly from the lips of the minister there can be no doubt as to the position. Then he went on:
The dominion government will be able, correspondingly, to reduce some of the burden it was prepared to assume for a public investment and social security programme.
Then last evening in this house, at page 5319 of Hansard, the minister had this to say:
The details of our original proposals may of course change as a result of further study or of developing public opinion or of discussion with provincial governments at a general conference which will be necessary' before they can be implemented. The proposed contributions which the dominion may be able to make in the field of public investment and social security may, as I have said publicly and as I advised the provinces which were negotiating with us last winter, have to be revised-
In that case the word "revised" means "reduced".
-to take into account the substantial increase in the financial payments which the dominion has now undertaken to make as rental for the tax fields in question.
My point in reading these quotations is this. The government made certain proposals to the provinces that it would undertake a great national programme. In its negotiations with the provinces it had to increase the size of its offers. This it did, as the minister frankly said, on two or three occasions. He said that having increased the government's contribution to the provinces, the provinces can now expect less from the government in the future.

Tax Agreements with Provinces
My sixth criticism last night was that this plan brought forward by the government abandons the principle of fiscal need. I think the minister's statement last night on fiscal need was a specious argument. There is one way to give fiscal need, and no other, namely to recognize the periodic, or in some cases, I am afraid:, the permanent, inability of some provinces to provide adequate standards of social services. That is one of two reasons given in justification of the kind of measure by which the dominion collects taxes from the people and gives some of it to provincial governments to spend. I support the government to a degree in that policy. But I agree with the Prime Minister's statement of past years that to go beyond that is a vicious principle.
There is one other thing I might have said, which I shall say now, it is this: This proposal or these related proposals are not charity, not merely taking; from a wealthy section of Canada and having the money distributed: in needy sections. It is not that only. In this federal state of ours, with nine provinces, the people in all these provinces contribute to the wealth made by large institutions, which by circumstances find themselves located in the larger centres of population in. the central parts of the country. The net result of that is that the taxing capacity of the outlying sections is reduced, and the taxing capacity of the central sections is increased. To the extent that that is so, any state is warranted in taking taxes where they can be obtained and allowing a part of them to be spent where they are needed, I did not mention this aspect last night; I am sure it was not necessary. I mention it now only because one might take from the discussion that this was wholly a charitable arrangement-one 'by which money was collected in the wealthy sections of our economy and spent, in other sections. It. is not wholly that. Some of the wealthiest sections of our economy have- been made such by wealth made in business done in other sections of the nation. It is entirely defensible to use some of that- to help correct- in a small way the inequities that result.
Let me conclude by this one statement. In my judgment the course the government is following means the liquidation of the dominion-provincial conference system which has been inherent in our confederation system since its inception. Certain provinces need help. That is granted. And help to a degree can be justified . But the procedure the government. has followed has brought about serious criticism. It is resulting in disunity and all the other objections I have raised. Certain provinces having undertaken to come into this 83166-3434
arrangement, we ought not to deny them that right. We can defend it to a point. Beyond that it is unsound policy.

Mr. Speaker, this party does not intend to make any long debate on this measure. In our opinion it is not a measure that one can get particularly hot about either way. We regret exceedingly that the dominion-provincial conference which was called in August, 1945, broke down and that now the arrangements between the dominion and the provinces are on a province-to-province basis. I can agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) that that is a bad aspect of our dominion-provincial relations.
I should like to draw attention to the fact that the dominion-provincial conference was called by the dominion government. The impression is abroad that the conference broke up because certain premiers were, to use the language of the street, playing politics. But even if that were so I do not think the dominion government is in a strong position when it refuses to call the conference together again. Because of the position of the dominion government, where it has an over-all view of the needs of Canada, knows what the needs are in every .part of the dominion, in fact knows that the provinces as a whole constitute the dominion and that there is no dominion of Canada outside the provinces, it should pocket its pride and, regardless of what the attitude of any provincial premier had been or might be in another provincial conference, call a new conference.
In my opinion the dominion government has all the trumps in this game, and it would be the easiest thing in the world to expose any provincial premier who tries to disrupt the over-all programme that the dominion government is attempting to put into effect. Therefore I do not believe the dominion government can be excused for the failure to call a dominion-provincial conference after the last one broke up in April or May of 1946.
Let me read two short paragraphs from the statement made by the Prime Minister on the first day of the conference, August 6, 1945. On page 6 of the proceedings of the plenary session of that date, the Prime Minister said:
Above all, we aim at the maintenance of a high level of employment and income. In no field are the interests of dominion and provinces more thoroughly one than in the maintenance at all times of a high level of employment. The fear of war is undoubtedly the worst of all fears in the minds of men today. But next to the fear of war, the greatest fear for most men is the fear of unemployment. There are men and women who almost dreaded the
Tax Agreements with Provinces

coming of victory because they feared that depression and unemployment might come in victory's train. That fear we must all seek, in close cooperation, to remove.
I agree with every word the Prime Minister said. The fear of unemployment cannot be removed by the arrangements that are now being made between government and government. That fear is just as prominent in the minds of the Canadian people in 1947 as it was in 1945. The Prime Minister went on to say:
Finally, our proposals are designed to make possible a comprehensive system of social insurance, partially federal and partially provincial, through which the community will share with the individual in meeting the variations of income and expense to which the rise and fall of business activity, natural disasters, accident, ill health and old age render all of us liable. Improved standards of nutrition, housing, health and social amenities, for both urban and rural populations, are also objectives of our reconstruction policy. Of these housing is a most urgent need in the period of reconstruction.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance or any member of the government: Have any of the problems mentioned by the Prime Minister in that paragraph been solved by any agreement that has been made up to date or that can be made under the present policy? Obviously the answer is no.
There is a little background to this whole question of which we should not lose sight. I am old enough to remember what happened at the end of world war I as well as at the end of world war II. At the end of both wars people had come to the conclusion, because of what we were able to do during those wars in the matter of production, that never again would we go back to the haphazard, unplanned way of providing for our needs. They felt that there had to be more planning and, as the Prime Minister so well said, a sharing by individuals who were in good circumstances with other individuals who were not. What we need is an over-all policy where the rich provinces will share with the poor provinces because all together are Canada.
I found some difficulty in following the reasoning of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), but that may be my fault and not his. I had the same difficulty last night and my difficulty was not decreased today. At page 5321 of yesterday's Hansard the leader of the opposition referred to the way in which the amounts needed by the provinces had been increased step by step. He said it was S40 million under the Rowell-Sirois commission; it was $117 million under the 1942 tax arrangements; it was $138 million under the 1945 proposal, $198 million under the 1946 proposal, and it is $228 million at the present time.

I think that is what my hon. friend said. However, I am not going to refer to it any more. I am in a quandary, now and I was in a quandary last night as to whether he was supporting or opposing this measure. I am wondering now just where he stands. I hope when I finish I shall not be in the same boat.
I should like to know what is meant by fiscal need. Does fiscal need mean the programme of social services and public investment which was mentioned in the 1945 proposals? In my opinion fiscal need means just that. Let us see what was in that programme. I shall refer only to the headings. There was a national health programme for all the provinces. There was provision for old age pensions to those seventy years of age and over, for which the dominion government would assume full responsibility without a means test. That would mean that everyone over seventy would automatically get a pen-
