sion. If he had income over and above the maximum amount of the income tax exemption, then the tax would take it away. For those old age pensioners between the ages of sixty-five and sixty-nine years the government would go fifty-fifty with the provinces on a means test basis.
Then there was provision for unemployment assistance benefits. I have not looked this up recently, but my memory is that those benefits were to cover persons not covered by unemployment insurance or who had exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits. TheD there was a policy of public investment. After a social security programme I think that a policy of public investment which would provide employment, which would increase the wealth of the country, is of equal importance to a social security programme under which benefits would be paid. In the one case benefits are paid, and in the other case we enable people to provide incomes for themselves. Of course the kind of social security programme that we would be able ultimately to provide for ourselves would depend upon the amount of wealth produced and the national income created by that wealth.
My criticism of the government's policy is that it does, as the leader of the opposition says, throw overboard the whole social security and public investment programme. I am inclined to believe that the government was pleased rather than otherwise that the conference broke down, because the psychology in favour of cooperation and state assistance in 1946 was not as strong as it was in 1945 and in the last years of the war. In 1946 the psychology of private enterprise was on the make-take what you can and the devil take the hindmost. I believe that the government had come to doubt its own programme and was glad when the premiers of two of the central provinces broke up the conference in 1946.	*
The leader of the opposition several times referred to the fact that the federal government in its taxing arrangements was encroaching upon provincial tax fields to such an extent that no field of taxation was now clear for the provinces. Let us take a look at that picture.
The Canadian constitution provides for a distribution of powers and responsibilities as between the dominion and the provinces. We found that during the depression years, with all the taxing powers that they had ever had, most of the provinces found themselves in a position where they could not discharge the responsibilities given to them under the British North America Act, and the federal government had to come to their assistance. That being so, I think it is far more important to the provinces that they should have sufficient income to enable them to discharge the responsibilities that they now have, regardless of where the money is to come from, than that they should have taxation fields which will not provide them with sufficient revenue to discharge those responsibilities. I do not believe that any province should be greatly disturbed if the dominion is collecting all the taxes, because the people who are paying the taxes are all Canadian citizens and they are the same people whether it is the dominion or the province that collects the tax. If there are two sets of tax collectors there will be two expense accounts to pay.
What is required is that the dominion and the provinces should come to an arrangement whereby each province would be provided with sufficient revenue to discharge the responsibilities that it assumed under whatever arrangement it entered into with the federal government. The present arrangements do not do that; they do not provide for social security services, and while we may get along without those services at the present time, perhaps in a few more years, maybe sooner, we shall be in the position in which we found ourselves between 1930 and 1939, when seven of the provinces of this dominion were not able to discharge the responsibilities assigned to them under the constitution.
In conclusion I would urge the government at the earliest possible moment to call the dominion-provincial conference. If pride deters them, let them throw it overboard. Big people' are not deterred by a little pride. When the conference is called together, if any premier of any province begins to use that conference as a political platform I am satisfied that the dominion government, if it wishes to go ahead with the programme outlined in the green book, has sufficient material to expose that individual and bring him to time. The people of his province will repudiate him if he puts them in such a position that they are not able to take advantage of benefits which they could enjoy if he accepted a reasonable arrangement with the dominion.

he did. There were some things in the speech of the hon. member who just preceded me (Mr. Maclnnis) with which I can also agree.
As is well known, Mr. Speaker, our group has always taken a strong position against centralization. We do so now. We feel that this is a move for centralizing control in the federal government. We do not think that that is in the interests of Canada and its strength, and in due course I am satisfied that whatever government may be in power at the time, it will come to recognize that centralization is not the answer and will take steps to see that Canada is strengthened by a decentralizing move. However, that is not what I wanted to develop at any length, except to place our position on record as strongly against centralization.
The agreements seem to be based on quite reasonable terms, at least in relation to conditions at the present time. I have no particular objection to the terms. But it must not be overlooked that the money which is being paid back in these increased grants to the provincial governments is collected out of taxes which come from the very people to whom the grants are being paid.
It is not a question of the provinces getting a better deal than they have ever had. It is simply a question of the provinces receiving from a central collection agency taxes which they could very well collect for themselves if they wished to tax their people that heavily. I am wondering, Mr. Speaker, what the dominion government would do should another disastrous unemployment situation arise. I went through that sort of thing in Alberta in the thirties and I know what it means to a province with limited revenues. It was not during that time a question whether we could collect taxes to take care of unemployment and the needs of hungry people. It was not that at all. The money just was not there. There were plenty of goods and services that could have been made available, but the money was not there. There was only one authority in this dominion of Canada that could have made that money available, but they did not do it.
Now I am wondering if, under the terms of this agreement, the federal government might not back out of the picture in case of the development of a serious unemployment situation and say to the provinces: We have provided for all that in this agreement, and it is your responsibility from now on; take it.
I protest against that most vehemently. I think the provinces will have to guard themselves against such a possibility and I hope they will. I can do no better, Mr. Speaker,

than to put on the record a statement made by the Hon. Mr. Manning, premier of Alberta, in his budget speech delivered on March 7, 1947, in the Alberta legislature. This sums up his attitude towards the whole agreement. It is the stand that we in this group will take in this house, because it is the stand that we have consistently followed. Mr. Manning said:
The government of Alberta is convinced that the accumulating force of circumstances will continue to add still further emphasis to the impossibility of a satisfactory permanent solution to the problem of dominion-provincial relations until three basic factors are recognized and acted upon. First, there must be a redefining and, if necessary, a reallocation of^ the rights and responsibilities of the respective governments in the light of conditions as they exist today.
Not as they existed, Mr. Speaker, back in 1867, but as they exist today'.
Second, each government must be assured adequate revenue under its own unfettered jurisdiction to enable it to discharge fully its constitutional responsibilities and provide adequately for the just requirements of its people. Third, to make this possible the Canadian monetary system must be reformed in the manner necessary to permit the monetization of the entire national production and the use of the financial credit thereby created to supplement and progressively to replace excessive taxation as a means of providing public revenue. The Alberta government will continue to do everything in its power to secure recognition of these basic factors to the end that this important problem, ultimately, will be solved in a manner satisfactory to the dominion and all the provinces, and on a basis that will assure the Canadian people the national and provincial economic stability which they desire and to which they are justly entitled.
That is the attitude of the government of my province with respect to these agreements. They do not look upon the arrangement as in any sense a permanent one. I think they are quite well satisfied at present with the terms of the agreements, but,I think too that I should emphasize that they signed the agreement with the reservation that it would be for a preliminary five-year period, and also on the understanding-I believe an undertaking was given by this government that would lend credence to their understanding-that one year prior to the termination of these contracts another conference would be held at which further efforts would be made to reach a permanent solution that would be satisfactory in the interests of all concerned.
In conclusion let me say this. I quite recognize the importance of social security measures and of public investment possibilities. I do not think, however, that it would be possible to conceive a better programme of social security and public investment than that which is embodied with in the terms of the

Tax Agreements with Provinces
statement which Mr. Manning made, particularly in the third provision, which I quote once more:
To make this possible, the Canadian monetary system must be reformed in the manner necessary to permit the monetization of the entire national production and the use of the financial credit thereby created to supplement and progressively to replace excessive taxation as a means of providing public revenue.
There you have the answer to our calls and demands for public investment and for social security agreements. The provinces, if given their rights under a proper monetary system, can provide their own social security, and they will not have to come here on their stomachs with hat in hand asking the federal govern-met to help them. They can provide their own public investment programme and take care of their own people if this government will sit down with them and work out a definition and perhaps an allocation of powers that will enable the provinces to discharge fully the responsibilities that are placed upon them under the terms of our constitution. I wanted to emphasize that as our position.

The Sanhedrin controls the spirit of the Winnipeg Free Press, and the Winnipeg Free Press in flesh and bone was John W. Dafoe. Mr. Dafoe was self-educated, but perhaps not absolutely enough. He could not give to his own brain the last finishing touch. But he was there and he probably wanted to organize something for the benefit of the prairie provinces. If ever anyone had the personal ways and, to use a royal expression, the personal style, to canvass the readers of his newspaper, he had. There was Mr. Rowell, and there was also Senator Crerar, a delightful man, who was then the Manitoba minister in the dominion government. My hon friend the leader of the opposition was then premier of the province which was so ably represented in the dominion cabinet by Mr. Crerar. So we have Mr. Crerar, Mr. Dafoe and Mr. Bracken. Naturally they wanted to have the whole scheme promoted by a premier of one of the nine provinces,

and they could not find any better man than the premier of their own province, who is now leader of the opposition.

Then the Sanhedrin wanted a judge to preside over the commission, a man who would be entirely disinterested; and according to the official figures I obtained he was well looked after. At the time he was not a judge; he was not a cabinet minister; he was not a member of parliament; he was not a civil servant, but in the ten years from 1927 to 1937 he received from the dominion government $168,332.51. In addition, from November 20, 1926, to June 14, 1928, he received an amount of $48,641.63 for services, travelling expenses, expenses, allocations and so on, not taking into account what was paid by other departments than justice and national revenue. So he received $216,000 in that period of ten years. He was full of disinterest. He was there as chairman of the commission; he had

Tax Agreements with Provinces
Mr. Dafoe sitting with him and another French-Canadian judge who was there for a time but who became sick-probably he became sick of it, though he was not in such bad health as the second chairman, who died not long after he was appointed. It was impossible to live in that atmosphere. It was babel at its worst. It was indeed a fiesta of the intelligentsia. They came from all over the world, a caravan of learned fellows with thick glasses, bringing statistics in brief cases which were well loaded with important documents. It was not paper they wanted; it was straw to make nests and feather to make pillows. They wanted to make themselves comfortable in the fine atmosphere of Ottawa.

subtopic: COMPENSATION TO PROVINCES IN LIEU OP INCOME AND OTHER TAXES
speechtext:
No; it was all generosity, abnegation and the spirit of sacrifice, and they forgot themselves completely. They were coming here to serve the country, this gentleman who had been paid $216,000 in ten years and all the rest. It was self-sacrificing abnegation. Then they organized that scheme, and we saw a mountain of reports. It was the Rowell commission. Strangely enough they recommended exactly what the Minister of Finance, Mr. Dunning, had suggested after the election in 1935-to take over succession duties and that sort of thing, Which I opposed many years ago when the matter was brought before the house.
The leader of the opposition has admirably summarized the recommendations contained in the report of the Rowell-Sirois commission: that the central government should collect taxes wherever they can be obtained, and that the provinces suffering from a poor economy should be benefited on the basis of fiscal need, that is, to the extent of the amount necessary to enable those provinces to have the same levels of public services as the other provinces without having to apply a higher level of taxation. His suggestion was that some provinces which he considered richer because they were not his own would have to be called upon to pay for the other provinces that were supposed to be not so fortunate; but the hon. gentleman also said the basic recommendation of that commission was that the provinces of Canada should be aided by the central government on the basis of fiscal need. It is very difficult to establish that; and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) asked for some information from the leader of the opposition, who also said, "In fact there are vast differences, so that we find in this nation six different major types of economy". I wonder if he perhaps missed a page in which
those six different major types of economy were described. I am very anxious to know what they are, and I hope that when the bill is in committee the hon. gentleman will be kind enough to tell us.
In the past, Mr. Speaker, it was stated that some of these provinces have not been able to secure as high a standard of living or of public services as the others. Those mentioned have been the prairie provinces and the mari-times. When it comes to helping any Canadian, whether he is from the east or from the west, there should be no objection. But there should be order in government, and the only way to have order in government is to have the same treatment for all. If some provinces both east and west have difficulty in making ends meet it is precisely because they do not have the powers of taxation that have been given them by the constitution. That constitution has been in force for eighty years, and until ten years ago there was no difficulty. At that time the difficulty came about not in the east but in the prairie provinces, and due to drought and other reasons, some of which may perhaps have been good reasons. They were given a palliative, just as though the government were ashamed to act properly toward the western provinces. Instead of saying, "You need something, and we will fix you up", it was always given by the back door. After a certain time the prairie provinces were most generously treated, especially after the Bennett regime went out. They were better treated than the eastern provinces; but the government seemed to be ashamed to do anything in the open. There was always a screen and a reason to hide what had been done. I had to ask special questions to get full information from the then Minister of Finance, Mr. Dunning, who seemed reluctant to give a true picture of what had been done for the western provinces.
What has been said1 about the inferiority of the maritime and the prairie provinces is an insult to the population of these provinces. The propaganda is to the effect that the older provinces, Ontario especially and Quebec, will have to pay the system of social security for the whole country. It seems that if the taxes had been adjusted; properly there would be no difficulty about social security in any part of the country.
When the motion to appoint the Rowell commission was brought before the house I remember that I uttered thunderous "hear, hears", and it was struck out from Hansard. The purpose of the motion was to bring some order in the relations between the dominion and the provinces. The purpose was

Tax Agreements with Provinces
excellent. If it was falsified by those who wanted to serve certain areas at the expense of the rest of the country. Mr. Speaker, you would be astonished to see the fabulous sums that have been paid for the Rowell-Sirois report, about half a million dollars at the time. But that is nothing compared with what we have to pay now.
In the summary of the report it is said that Ottawa wall be able to collect more taxes than the provinces ever could. That is one of the arguments that have been brought out by the commission. But, sir, the reason that I am opposed to it is that I consider that the collection of taxes is something most unpleasant and it should be left to those who spend the money. I do not see why Ottawa should have the opprobrium of collecting taxes and pass the amount over to the provinces. That is one reason. Besides that it is an occasion for red tape to show up. There are many reasons why I cannot understand that policy, and I wonder whether all the difficulties which have been raised in regard to dominion-provincial relations have not been caused by the bureaucrats who have taken advantage of the Rowell-Sirois report to fatten themselves at the expense of the public treasury. You know very well, sir, that it is most difficult to make some people who have been appointed on a temporary basis understand that as soon as their time is ended they will have to go. When someone is employed as a temporary in Ottawa it is for the duration of his life. What we see now is the old struggle. It is not a fight between the provinces and Ottawa; it is the old struggle between the taxpayer and the bureaucrat, and the bureaucrats are much more numerous here than they are in the provinces.
Why not consider the question objectively? Those who made the report wanted to make it big and thick to impress those who would never read it. It is a well known fact that not one out of ten thousand people has read the full report of the Rowell-Sirois commission. But when the report is so big it creates a deep impression on the people, even on those who do not know how to read and write. It would have been much better for this country if some of the university professors and journalists who worked on the report had never been taught how to read and write. Therefore, sir, I have always agreed with the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in his statements of 1929 and 1930 when he said, as was quoted by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Bracken):
That it was a thoroughly vicious system to have one body raise taxes and another body expend the money thus secured.
[Mr. Pouliot.l
On February 5 of this year, I offered my services as an intermediary between the dominion and the provinces to try to get them to come to an understanding so that we would have order in. this country and so that grants which are made to the provinces should no longer be considered as bribes but given as due. If we look at the British North America Act we shall see the equal treatment which was given the first four provinces at confederation. Naturally each province did not have as much, but the proportion was the same for all, and so long as the same proportion of money is paid to all provinces it is difficult to have an objection to it, although it is much better and economically sounder to give the provinces the opportunity to collect their own taxes and to do what they think they have to do with their own money. It is a question of decentralization. Decentralization is a Liberal principle. It is the principle of giving the same opportunity to all in every part of the country. That is the way in which the country was governed at the time of Alexander Mackenzie, at the time of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and at the time of Mackenzie King before Bennett came to power. I remember those happy days when the country was fortunate and when everybody seemed to be prosperous even in spite of the crash of 1929.
If I took the trouble to speak about this today it was not with the expectation to convert anybody right now, but it was to afford all hon. members the opportunity to think over what has been said. I may be right; I may be wrong. I am not prejudiced, but I hope that in the near future the quarrels between some provinces and Ottawa will stop. I find it a disgrace. The provinces are considered wrong because they do not accept the views of this government, because they are not ready to accept what has been cooked up in the Rowell-Sirois report.
It is not a question of so many more millions .to be given by Ottawa, because I submit that the provinces have a right to expect that the same proportion will be paid to all. When it is done to all the provinces there can be no question of bribing. I can remember that not later than last year the question came up of giving other countries some large gifts which would have to be paid out of taxes. Members of parliament were told, "If you do not vote for this, you will not have family allowances any longer." If that is not blackmail, I do not know what blackmail is. That was not said by the present minister; it was said by. someone else who was putting undue pressure.
That is not the way to act with the provinces. The provinces have a right to be

Tax Agreements with Provinces
proud and dignified because they have exclusive rights within their jurisdiction under the British North America Act. I need not refer hon. members to the various provisions of that imperial statute because they know that the provinces on the one hand, and the dominion on the other have exclusive jurisdiction respectively. That means that the provinces are the equal of the dominion in their respective fields. The dominion is asking the provinces to make a concession in connection with taxing powers and in return -the provinces will be given the returns from the collection of those taxes. It cannot go on like that. Let the provinces be independent; let Ottawa be independent, but let us all be friendly. I hope that in the near future, with the fine disposition of the Minister of Finance who is open-minded and broadminded, and with the equally fine disposition of the premiers who have not accepted the proposals, there will be a complete revision of what has been done with seven provinces. This should be done at the earliest possible opportunity in order that all the provinces can be treated fairly and squarely.
If the leader of the opposition has reached this conclusion, I congratulate him. I do not know how he will vote. His speech was based on the false principle of gifts. I am against gifts to provinces as I am against gifts to other countries. The provinces should be given the right to maintain themselves through their own taxation.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, the title of the bill is rather long but it is fully descriptive. It is styled:
An act to authorize the government of Canada to enter into agreements with the governments of the provinces pursuant to which, in return for compensation, the provinces agree to refrain from levying certain taxes for a limited period.
As its title indicates, this bill entails the surrender by the provinces to the dominion, for a period at least, of certain constitutional rights. It suggests that among some of the provinces there are necessities which should be met. As a preface to what I have to say, I should like to make two definite statements. The first is that I believe that, as a civilized community, it behooves Canada so to administer its affairs, in conjunction with the provinces, that need may be relieved where it exists. I do not wish anything I say to be interpreted as hostile to a revision of taxing rights and to a reallocation between the dominion and the provinces of the revenue of those taxes. The next statement is that these questions are not free from' controversy. It is possible for men to hold divergent views, to hold them in good faith and with some degree of enlightenment. For
that reason I was sorry to hear the acting leader of the C.C.F. group state this afternoon that two premiers-there were three a short time ago-

speechtext:
My hon. friend would be prophetic; if he were better acquainted with the attachment to principle of the people of the province in which is located the county I represent, he would not be quite as certain of the accuracy of the allegation he has made. Be that as it may, I am sorry that the hon. gentleman who leads the C.C.F. group found it necessary to characterize the attitude of two or three premiers as political. If my ears did not mislead me, he said that they had been playing politics. I would be loath to make that suggestion in view of the sound arguments which were advanced by each of those gentlemen at the conference and, forsooth, because of many convictions which I hold myself. One of the characteristics of this chamber and of our political institutions is that a man may state views which may not be universally accepted, without his motives being challenged.
This bill, if enacted, will enable the federal government to pay to the provinces the sums of money stated in the bill, the consideration being that the provinces yield for a period of time their right to levy certain taxes. The policy of taxing by one authority and spending by another is false in principle and wasteful in practice. It has been condemned by all authorities, including Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and by none more roundly, more completely, more forcefully and more eloquently, than by the right hon. gentleman who leads this house.
We are told that agreements have been entered into separately with seven of the nine provinces. In several instances these agreements have been renegotiated because a province, finding that some other province had subsequently to its arrangement with the dominion, received better terms, came back and insisted that it be given terms as satisfactory as those conceded to the last province- with which the dominion had dealt.
I should like to .make it quite clear that my objection to this method of dealing with the provinces rests on what I believe to be a principle. This country's genesis, this country's beginning, this country's origin as a confederation rests on conference, on agreements arrived at in the open, and if we are to put an end to the era of conference and agreement which makes it obligatory that all the provinces should be treated in a way which is satisfactory to all, then I fear that we have come upon very sad days for this dominion.

Tax Agreements with Provinces
How are we to deal with each of these provinces separately? What are we contending for; what is the group which sits to my immediate left contending for as well as other groups in the house in the field of labour? It is that everybody should have complete freedom of bargaining. Is one to believe that a province whose necessities are extremely urgent has the same freedom of bargaining the same power and capacity to bargain with respect to its own interests as a province which has a relatively larger revenue?
To take a case, let us take that of Nova Scotia; let us remember that only a short time ago an announcement was made in the house that the province of Nova Scotia had finally accepted the offer which had been made to it by the dominion. Here are the words of the premier of Nova Scotia only a little over a year ago. At page 419 of the Dominion and Provincial Submissions and Plenary Conference Discussions he said this:
In return we are asked to surrender our rights to collect income and corporation taxes, two fields which, as I said, yielded last year something in excess of one and a half billion dollars. We have then to surrender the rights to collect income and corporation tax, two fields which I said last year yielded something over one billion and a half dollars. That is the position which the provinces are asked to take. Let me ask you, Mr. Chairman, and the delegates here, whether they represent the dominion government or the provinces, let me ask anyone who is within sound of my voice, let me ask that greater body to which we as public servants are all accountable, the citizens of our provinces or of Canada, let me ask any of those people whether they think that is a fair or honourable or dignified position in which to place the provinces in this dominion. Provincial autonomy will be gone. Provincial independence will vanish. Provincial dignity will disappear. Provincial governments will become mere annuitants of Ottawa. Provincial public life-and I do not think these words are too strong-will be debased and degraded. I cannot think that such a state of affairs is desired by the representatives of the government of Canada here today, my one-time colleagues. I am sure that they have no wish or desire to see such a state of affairs come to pass in this country, nor can I believe that such a state of affairs is desired by the people of this country.
Yet the same hon. gentleman, if we are to believe what has been stated in the house, has signed an agreement with the dominion. He has had to yield up the dignity of provincial life. He has had to foreswear the autonomy in which he believed. Why? Because he and his people have been starved into that acquiescence. I say, Mr. Speaker, that agreements which rest upon a basis of that kind are insecure; they are not durable, and they will not bring about a happy, contented or prosperous Canada.
[Mr. Hackett.l
The taxing powers under the constitution have been divided between the federal and the provincial authorities. It is now sought so to divide them that the federal government may collect the taxes and pay over large sums to the provinces. That system is subversive of the whole idea of confederation and it will make, as has been said by the premier of Nova Scotia, vassals of the provinces. I submit that it is far better that a dominion-provincial conference be called together and that an arrangement be arrived at with all the provinces whereby each province, retain* ing its right to tax within the terms of the constitution, shall provide by direct taxation for its own needs.
How did this difficulty come about? We have heard this afternoon something said about the Rowell-Sirois report. At the time that study was undertaken the provinces were in the greatest distress. That situation has been modified. The party that now needs money most urgently is the dominion. The dominion, having acquired taxing rights from the provinces for a period of time, having enjoyed them for the duration and for the purpose only of winning the war, directed them to another purpose. It. used them to win an election. It used the proceeds of the taxing rights conceded to it by the provinces for the purpose of winning the war for the purpose of providing family allowances. Family allowances are an excellent thing. Dishonesty is not a virtue. When a government is in possession of certain borrowed taxing rights and revenues for a specific purpose and it diverts them to another purpose, it seems to me it is nothing short of dishonest, Filial piety is a fine thing itself, but were a young man to break into the home of a neighbour and take away a large sum of money and, with a portion of it, buy an armchair or an automobile for his parents, his conduct would hardly be lauded.
That is exactly what has happened here. But that is not all. At the end of the period, when the time came to return to the provinces their taxing rights, the dominion said: We cannot do that because, if we do, we shall not be able to continue these social services, social services which were excellent in themselves but which, in reality were within the jurisdiction of the provinces, which, upon a proper reallocation of the taxing privileges, were better equipped and better able to provide those services than was the dominion itself.
We have found that the dominion received something over $2 billion from the exercise of these taxation rights. It paid out to the provinces, as the leader of my party said last

night, about SI 17 million per annum during the war, keeping the balance for it-s own purpose. The amount has increased rapidly since that time. It was SI 17 million during the war, $138 million in 1945, $198 million in 1946, and according to the table which the Minister of Finance put on Hansard last night, it will be $228 million for 1947. There is evidence of the unsatisfactory result following the method which the government has pursued. It has made a secret arrangement with one province and another secret arrangement with another province, and when the first province has found out what has happened it has required a larger amount of money.

speechtext: We are not a Tory party.

subtopic: COMPENSATION TO PROVINCES IN LIEU OP INCOME AND OTHER TAXES
speechtext:
As to the secrecy, they were not made openly in public conference; they were not made with the knowledge of all the provinces; and the point I am endeavouring to make, Mr. Speaker, is that any arrangement with a province which is made outside, the knowledge of all the provinces, any arrangement which is made in the absence of any member of the family, is a secret arrangement and one which tends to undermine the very basis of confederation, one which makes for rivalries and jealousies and for misunderstanding throughout the country.
We have just about emerged from a period of sordid division which has prevailed throughout the land since the first great war. It is not my intention to go into all the details of that sad story which grew out of the question of where Canada's duty lay. with regard to defence. You know, Mr. Speaker, that the situation was such that a large element, a very respectable and intelligent element in one section of the country was told and told frequently that it had no duty to serve anywhere unless this country were attacked. We are through with that. The fallacy of those statements has been brought home to those wiho made them. It was only the other day that we enacted in this house legislation to provide for tribunals before which members of visiting forces who had misconducted themselves might be haled, meaning, if it meant [DOT] anything, that visiting forces would come to Canada for the purpose of coordinating their military endeavour with our own, so that our country might be, if not immune from attack, made strong in resisting it.
Now we are at last free from the divisions which arose out of enforced military service,
are we to be injected into a new era of division in the economic area by permitting the government again to rule by means of dividing? Are we to permit the government to make arrangements with individual provinces? Is each province to be put on the block and to be bid in according to its necessity or the whim of him who has the moneybag?
This whole idea of centralizing taxation is bringing to Canada a theory and practice which are entirely contrary to the scheme of government which was developed and enacted eighty years ago; and if we are to continue, as my leader said, to permit the centralizing of the taxing power and of the spending agencies in Ottawa we are imperilling confederation. The interests of this country are too diverse. Our origins, our outlook, our hopes are so far apart that they cannot find expression in a unitary form of government. We can only hope to exist if complete and continuing provincial autonomy be preserved in this country.
We have been led astray to some extent,
I think, by the use of words. I noticed that the minister last night referred to the "rental of fields of taxation". That is not exactly a new phrase. It is rather a glittering one, and it is certainly a loose one. It is not unlike that other term used by a master of words, "lend-lease", which was really an aphorism to describe acts of war, while the semblance of peace was maintained. I say again that the words "rental of fields of taxation" are misleading. We are witnessing the transfer of provincial rights to the dominion. It is all very well to talk of it in terms of rental; but, once an act of this description is perpetrated, it is difficult to undo it. In my hand I have the report of the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations, and the last words found in the first volume-which is really the last volume, because it is the report-indicate the aim of the transfer and make clear how final is the step that will be taken if this bill be passed. Here are the words found at page 259:
Where legislative power over a particular subject matter is divided, it is ordinarily desirable that these powers should be pooled under the control of a single government in order to secure unified effort in administration.
And on the same page in a preceding paragraph we find these words:
Thus the dominion must always hesitate long before withdrawing a grant. The provinces know this and they are not seriously impressed by threats of such action. The power to withdraw the grant is not an effective sanction except against the most flagrant of abuses.
Tax Agreements with Provinces

So that we can draw but small consolation from the fact that this is only a five-year agreement. When these moneys have been paid and this method of dealing with the provinces has been established we shall, I fear, have gone just one step farther toward complete centralization of administration and centralizing of taxation in this dominion. The result will mean rivalry, dissatisfaction and waste; it will mean that the provinces will be weakened and will be forced, as Nova Scotia was forced, to accept the terms of the dictator, the centralizer, the powerful totalitarian who holds the purse strings.

I hear hon. gentlemen opposite dissenting. I naturally do not wish and cannot hope to force my views on anyone. I merely wish to express them. But when that dissent comes from hon. gentlemen from my own province, I marvel at their temerity; because if there is an element in this country which is interested in the maintenance of the integrity of the constitution, if there is an element in this country which needs the British North America Act and needs the power given to it by the constitution to develop its own institutions, to advance its own culture, to interpret its own soul, it is the element represented by the hon. gentlemen who sit opposite. I for one would feel remiss in the duty which is vested in me by my electors did I not say these few words against the terms of the bill and against the philosophy which underlies it.
I say again that our constitution found its genesis in understanding and in conference. Everyone who knows the story of Canada will recall that in 1866 only the two Canadas and Nova Scotia seemed willing to come into confederation. New Brunswick was not interested then. It was not until after what were called the Fenian raids, after the fear of invasion had arisen, that the latter province Changed its mind and decided that it would participate in the strength and power which come from brotherhood, understanding and complete disclosure. Could confederation ever have been .achieved if the fathers had gone about knocking at one door of each province? This dominion could never have been born had it not been for the endless conferences and a fathomless spirit of trust and faith which the various provinces placed in each other.
I want to say just one word before I take my seat. No one has greater awareness than I of the transcendant abilities of the right hon. gentleman who leads this parliament. But when his story is told, free from all propa-
ganda and all prejudice, I think it will be said that his genius-his sorry genius at times -has found expression in the creation of situations which the Canadian people were frequently unable to resist, although these situations were neither helpful to nor healthy for them. I reiterate what I said a moment ago about family allowances. The' people wanted family allowances; to get them they had to sacrifice provincial autonomy and accept centralized authority in this government.

That is a pertinent question. I am not going to vote for the bill which is now before the house, if it comes to a vote. I did not vote for family allowances, and I would not have voted for them had I been here because I believe it was a mistake in principle to introduce them as they were introduced, a mistake that will cost all the provinces of this country dearly, and none more than the province of Quebec. Only a short time ago this house was asked to pass a resolution, which resulted in an amendment to the constitution. Thus was another situation created! The. good province of Quebec was to have eight more seats in this house than it had before; and for that mess of pottage the members opposite consented, by a mere expression of party whim, by a mere parliamentary majority, that that sacred thing, the constitution, might be torn up.

Mr. GEORGES H. HEON (Argenteuil): Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that the government should have waited until the last days of an already quite long session to introduce this bill. As a matter of fact, I feel that none of the measures which have been put forward during the session now nearing its end, was more important than the one which is before us today. This bill, if it is favourably considered by the house, will enable the central government to enter into agreements with the provincial governments, pursuant .to which the provinces, for a consideration, will sell their already limited direct taxation powers, with a redemption right apparently exercisable after five years. The language of the bill is by no means clear, because of the ambiguity of the definition of the "value of gross national product"-which will apparently be the value as estimated by the dominion statistician by "methods generally recognized as the accepted
statistical techniques"-and because of the highly intricate calculations by means of which the compensation to be paid will be determined. I doubt whether the Canadian ratepayers who, after all, will once again have to pay for the proposed compensations, as they always have, will, unless they are well up in mathematics be able to make or understand the complicated calculations whereby they will take with one hand what they afterwards will give away with the other.
However, if the proposed measure is difficult to understand as regards definitions and figures, it suddenly becomes quite clear when enumerating the constitutional rights which the provinces will have to relinquish if they want to obtain further subsidies. To put it briefly, the measure requires the provinces to renounce their definite constitutional right to levy personal income taxes, corporation income taxes, and, in the language of the bill itself "corporation taxes as defined in the agreement", as well as their right to levy succession duties, if they want to obtain further subsidies. Moreover, while that is not stated in the bill, we may easily conclude or at least surmise, that the provinces unwilling to accept the proposed bargain can expect the central government to keep on levying the taxes which the provinces are required to give up, but without any compensation for the latter. Anyone familiar with the more or less satisfactory financial position of some provinces whose taxation revenue is far from large, can understand that the temptation to barter their constitutional prerogatives for gold is too great to be long resisted. To those who believe in a greater fiscal and economic centralization, in cyclic finance, in ever-increasing subsidies, the proposed measure appears most advisable. I do not question in the least the good faith or the sincerity of those who hold such views; however, I do not agree with that doctrine as I have frequently indicated by my speeches and my votes in this house, because I believe, in the first place, that centralization, even if based on the best grounds cannot, if continually extended, but lead to socialism, which, as we know, does not favour overmuch private initiative and free enterprise. We can easily imagine where such a centralizing policy would lead, should our socialist friends assume power, as they so often think they will some day..
Mr. Speaker, because I believe in dencen-tralization, both legislative and administrative, owing to our immense territory, the multiplicity and diversity of our natural resources, the particular needs of our ethnical group, settled mainly in the province of Quebec, with its praiseworthy and distinctive culture and traditions; because I also especially believe

Tax Agreements with Provinces
that provincial rights, already restricted by our constitution and encroached upon to a considerable extent during two wars, must be protected instead of being auctioned off to the highest bidder. I see in this piece of legislation, another serious menace: the present policy is the clever but far-reaching continuation of a policy initiated during the first world war, by which the dominion government, at a slow though deliberate pace infringes more and more upon provincial sources of revenue. Should this policy be pursued any longer-and it will seemingly be perpetuated in spite of everything-the provinces, some having almost reached that point already, would be completely at the mercy of the dominion government in the matter of fiscal needs.
To my mind, such is not the spirit and even less the basis of the federal pact. Our authorities in constitutional law, in the Quebec universities, at any rate, have always taught, and our courts have often emphasized that our constitution rests on the autonomy of the provinces in their own spheres. Some people, knowing that the fiscal rights of the provinces are limited to direct taxation and that incomes and profits are the main sources of this method of taxation, realize that the surrender of these sources to the dominion government, even at a huge price, can neither be approved nor promoted by supporters of autonomy and decentralization. I do not hesitate to state that I have always belonged to that school of thought, even before I entered parliament and before the Hon. Mr. Duplessis became premier of my province.
For Quebec particularly, each constitutional right surrendered represents a real danger, perhaps not so much for the time being as for the future. In fact, considering the new ideas afloat, which lead almost inevitably to absolute socialism and the omnipotent state taking over all economic and financial activities, considering also the veiled hostility forever smouldering in certain quarters against Quebec and French Canadians, do we know what the future has in store for us, and more especially, what will be the complexion of future dominion governments?
I have already said and take pleasure in repeating that personally, at any rate, I prefer the guarantees and rights granted by our constitution to the good will and possible sympathy of future dominion governments. Mr. Speaker, six provinces, after months of bargaining and overbidding, felt that they ought to sign an agreement based on the surrender of their rights: no doubt they acted after serious consideration, free from all compulsion,

I hope, and convinced that they had taken the right course. Although I am indeed most happy that, by holding back, they finally secured tidy sums of money, I cannot approve of the methods, tactics and procedures followed with respect to the presentation and signing of the agreements.
However, one should not conclude from what I have said that I am opposed to the payment of new and more substantial subsidies to needy provinces. I have a great deal of admiration and respect for Canadians of all racial origins who have settled in the west, and also for the courageous maritimers who have played a most glorious part in the history of our country. I readily agree that they were treated unfairly in the past and despite the fact that their population is smaller and their sources of taxation less numerous, they are nevertheless entitled to the same social security, the same full employment, and the same general services as the provinces whose population and revenues are larger. I would approve with much pleasure and satisfaction an agreement under which the dominion government and the more favoured provinces would agree to pay to provinces actually in need subsidies which they could justify, after collecting all the taxes they reasonably can. Every Canadian will approve the payment of additional subsidies to those provinces which can show their real need for them; however, I cannot agree that those same provinces should be placed in a situation where they have to sell, surrender, loan or rent acquired and fundamental rights in order to obtain that to which they are inalienably entitled.
Mr. Speaker, La Cliambre de Commerce de Montreal, which no one can, in good faith, charge with electoral propaganda or partiality, submitted through sheer patriotism and a sincere desire to help the government, a brief on the ticklish matter of dominion-provincial fiscal relations. The report had been previously unanimously adopted by the executive council of the chamber on April 2, 1947. I wish to stress the fact that I agree with the recommendations set forth in the report, and that my views on the legislation under consideration are practically the same as those of the Chambre de Commerce. For instance, on pages 3 and 4 of section No. 1 of the brief, the Chambre de Commerce states the following:
La Chambre de Commerce is of the opinion that the present dominion proposals would entail too large an economic and fiscal centralization. However, it considers that it would be urgent to put forth clear proposals satisfactory to all concerned, governments and taxpayers.

Tax Agreements with Provinces
And further:
The present legislative procedure constitutes, by its definition, at least partial centralization, not only with respect to collection of taxes, but also to legislative initiative in the field of taxation, which hinders the free use of the rights guaranteed the provinces by the constitution. One must not forget that the constitution limits the powers of the provinces to direct taxation and that a direct taxation policy rests upon the right to tax income and profits. For the above reasons, the Chambre de Commerce is opposed to such centralization.
And I conclude with another quotation from the same brief:
Unfortunately, it is impossible to ensure sufficiently uniform conditions as between one province and another without a certain contribution of subsidies, but the Chambre de Commerce is of the opinion that it should be restricted as much as possible.
Any province which has not yet decided to relinquish all taxation powers in the fields covered by the agreements should not authorize the carrying out of a federal permanent plan on economic control and social security, if, in order to maintain its constitutional rights it must, five years later, withdraw from and thereby disorganize such a plan.
On page 5 of the same section, the brief suggests the following basis of negotiations:
Both federal and provincial governments should come to an agreement which would clearly define their respective fields of direct taxation, according to their respective rights and needs, on the basis of the following fundamental principles-
(a)	Each government to keep the power of initiating legislation in the taxation fields granted to it by the constitution, which is the only system consistent with the exercise of the rights pertaining to their respective jurisdictions;
(b)	Provincial governments, being confined to the field of direct taxation, should be given the assurance that they may cultivate it according to their needs.
(c)	The various governments should devise means to simplify tax collection and to exchange information on ways and means of simplifying or standardizing legislation.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I ask my hon. friends to the left as well as to the right not to interpret my attitude as being prompted by picayune electioneering motives. I am not voting against this measure because it is brought down by a Liberal federal administration, nor, despite what some hon. members may think, because the Quebec provincial administration, under the leadership of Premier Duplessis, takes a definite stand on provincial autonomy, but for the simple and only reason that I have always looked upon legislative and fiscal decentralization as the policy best suited to serve and to protect the interests of the people in the future. I would oppose this bill, were it presented by a Conservative or other federal administration. I
would be on the side of any Liberal provincial administration which would advocate the policy of decentralization and autonomy in which I believe. After these remarks, no one doubts, I hope, that I shall vote against the bill,

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the second reading of this bill I wish to call the attention of the house and the minister to the fact that, although it provides for compensation for the nine provinces of Canada in consideration of their refraining from levying income and other taxes, there is no mention of remuneration or compensation for Yukon. For a few years, Yukon received a grant of money in compensation for that, but that was discontinued and has not been resumed. The reason given by the federal government for not resuming compensation to Yukon is that the territory makes a profit on the sale of liquor. speechtext:
I wish to speak for just five or ten minutes on this section. I intended to say something on the second reading, but perhaps I can express my views on this clause. First of all, I should like to point out two or three facts in connection with this subject. The bill before the committee is one of considerable importance to me, representing as I do a city which is a large tax-paying corporation in Canada. This bill empowers the government to enter into agreements with the governments of the provinces, pursuant to which agreements, in return for compensation, the provinces agree to refrain from levying certain taxes for a limited period.
This whole problem of taxation was covered bj- the British North America Act. At that time there were no motor cars and no telephones; there was no radio; there was nothing of that kind, and the British North America Act was looked upon then as something after the fashion of the law of the Medes and Persians. It could not be changed. At confederation certain powers were vested in the provinces, and the municipal systems that came into being then were, one might say, almost an afterthought of the intentions of the founders of confederation. As a result of the system adopted then, we have overgovernment and overtaxation in the country now. We have a duplicate system, provincial and municipal, foisted1 on the country, with taxing powers. As a matter of fact, we have a triplicate system, federal, provincial and municipal. The bill we have before us tonight indicates the necessity for constitutional reform. This was admitted in all the discussions that led to the appointment of the Rowell-Sirois commission. I may say that I introduced a motion dealing with parliamentary, cabinet and constitutional reform, and1 the minister of justice of that day arose and said that he would appoint a royal commission. Such a commission was appointed with Chief Justice Rowell as its first chairman; later on he was succeeded by Mr. Sirois, and that commission, which has come to be known as the Rowell-Sirois commission, functioned for two or three years.
If this bill is to be the law for a short period; if this legislation is temporary, in my opinion it sounds the death-knell of the provincial system. We are virtually empowering the provinces to impose taxation, but we are also taking away from them certain powers they have. It gives Ontario only $67 million.
From confederation down to the year 1917, income tax was the exclusive prerogative of the municipalities, and many federal burdens, following confederation, were placed upon the municipalities which the fathers of confederation had not intended. The result was that the municipalities had that form of taxation down to 1917, when Sir Thomas White was Minister of Finance, and they objected to the dominion invading their field at the time. But they were told it was just to be for a year or two during the war and when the war was over it was intended to be the end of it. But they still hung on to it.
We now come to the province. There was no income tax in the province before. It was the exclusive field of the municipality. But after the action taken by the dominion government with regard to income tax in 1917, the province came along and imposed a tax of a mill on the dollar of assessment on the municipalities and raised a large sum of money in our city at the time. It was a burden on real estate from 1917 to 1921. I want to point out in connection with this item that we must be careful that we do not adopt the principle which caused the separation of the American colonies from the mother country, namely, taxation without representation. That is a principle which is largely wrapped up in this bill. What I wish to see is the policy of confederation with regard to taxation. I believe, for confederation, in the old Cornish battle-cry, "Each for all and all for each." I believe that in this bill there has been the greatest invasion of the rights of the municipalities and the provinces. Ontario seems to be the forgotten province.
In connection with the merits of this bill, the allotment of the province is $67,000,000. When you look at the return of the Minister of National Revenue in the blue book, at pages 24 andi 25, and see the returns from the income and excise taxes, it is a large sum of money running into $423 million. In connection with income tax the tables are set out at pages 897,

Tax Agreements with Provinces
898 and 899 of the last issue of the Canada Year Book. I will not read the figures. The province of Ontario has been discriminated against. The taxation clauses of the Sirois report are unfair to our province and to Quebec. According to a return I saw, those two provinces pay about seventy per cent, of the total taxes of the whole dominion. There are certain provinces which one might call "have" provinces and there are two of them. Then there are certain provinces one might call 'have not" provinces. The "have not" provinces have been given a large share of the funds of this bill. I wish to say that Ontario is the forgotten province.
In conclusion, may I say in connection with these agreements that I hope they will be only temporary. They are interfering with all the municipalities. The municipalities are starving. They cannot have any money left under the system of taxation we have, which is a system which I described as that of robbing Peter to pay Paul, and under which the finances of the "have not" provinces are loaded on to the "have" provinces. How the municipalities are to live, I do not know. They are all having a hard fight, There are high taxes on real estate and on personal property. When you see that form of taxation which the municipalities have relied upon in order to get public buildings roads and public utilities, libraries, more schools and many social services, being assessed for social services by the dominion and province, it is a heavy burden. If it is only temporary, it is another matter. But on behalf of a large tax-paying city I protest against this way of handing out moneys and dealing wdth agreements. There are two forms of agreement in the bill. One is a statutory agreement under the British North America Act, with statutory subsidies paid. Then you add on to that what you might call politics. Politics is the science of government. A large number of others have been added on by statute from time to time regarding Prince Edward Island, Manitoba, provincial subsidies, Alberta natural resources, Railway Act, Manitoba resources, Saskatchewan and the maritimes. Our province seems to be the forgotten one when it comes to this.
I believe that charity should begin at home and that the two industrial provinces should have enough to live on. At the present time they have not; nor have the municipalities. The result is that taxes are a burden on industry, labour and capital. There should be some way of lessening that. We should be able to adopt a better system than the one we have, which is a haphazard system of handing out in some form varying amounts of money, with no standard agreement and no equality of treatment.

I take strong exception to that description. There has been no secrecy about the negotiations with the seven provinces which have so far evinced their intention of signing agreements with the dominion. In my explanatory statement last evening on the second reading of the bill I outlined in considerable detail and in chronological order the various steps which led up to the conclusion of these agreements. Any discussions with any particular province have been promptly made known to the other provinces with which the dominion was negotiating, and, moreover, have been made known promptly to all provinces, even those which up to the present time have evinced no particular desire to enter into agreements with the dominion. I could refer particularly, of course, to the negotiations which took place last December with the premier of British Columbia, in which he placed before the dominion government the views of his province with respect to these agreements and following which, speaking broadly, it was decided that we would extend to that province the benefit of the escalator clause which had been made available to the other provinces. That understanding or agreement was conditional upon the provinces which had already evidenced t-heir desire to enter into agreements. on the basis of the original budget proposals being prepared to agree; and that offer was promptly made known to those other provinces. As I stated last night, they put forward the view that under those circumstances they felt their position should be reconsidered. It was reconsidered and in January'-I have not the exact date before me-the new formula or new formulae which we worked out were made known to all the provinces.
I cannot emphasize too strongly that there have beep no secret, hole-in-the-corner negotiations with anyone. The circumstances which made it necessary for the dominion to make an offer to the provinces in the budget speech of last year on an individual basis have been fully outlined, and there is no reason for me
to review them now. But there has been no concealment, no secrecy, and no attitude of cynicism on the part of the dominion government in presenting these proposals to the provinces.	[DOT]
As I listened to the hon. member for Stanstead, knowing the interest he has in history I thought to myself there is nothing new under the sun. I remembered a letter which had been written by Sir John A. Macdonald to Hon. Joseph Howe in 1869, at the time confederation was being worked out and when agreements were being made between the various provinces. I sent out a note to the librarian, asking him to send me the letters of Sir John as collected by Joseph Pope; and I think it might be of passing interest if I were to quote from a letter written oh January 12, 1869. I need not read the whole letter; some of it relates to other matters, but it does have to do with the negotiations which were going on at that time concerning financial arrangements between the provinces of the new confederation of Canada. This is the third paragraph of the letter. The letter itself is a very interesting document, and I commend it to all hon. members. It is to be found at page 83 of the "Correspondence of Sir John Macdonald, 1840-1891", as collected by Sir Joseph Pope. He is referring to Sir John Rose, who was then Minister of Finance.
Rose, who will give you this, will meet you with a strong and sincere desire to come to some satisfactory arrangement. I need not, however, caution an experienced statesman like yourself, not to ask for too much. We shall have our own difficulties with the general parliament in carrying any concessions. Already has George Brown, through the Globe, protested against any pecuniary advantages being given to Nova Scotia, beyond those secured to them by the Union Act. This course will not at all deter us here from agreeing to what is reasonable, and staking our existence upon it in the legislature.
The province of Quebec, whose government is the reverse of economical, will, we fear, attempt to put on the screws for additional pecuniary aid if it is granted to you. So you see that we must take great care as to every step we take.
I have no doubt that you and Rose will find common standing ground, but whatever you agree upon must be kept strictly a secret. If divulged prematurely, the opposition press in Ontario will protest against any additional charges being put upon the people of that province. which, it is alleged, from its greater wealth, already hears more than its fair Bhare of the public burdens. In Quebec, the united press will demand a slice for that province, and all the anti-papers in Nova Scotia will denounce the arrangement as being altogether insufficient and unsatisfactory, and you will have the usual charge brought aganst you of "selling your heritage for a mess of pottage," etc.
It will be very difficult I know, for you, on your return, to resist the pressure of your friends to disclose the arrangement; but the answer should be satisfactory, that any arrangement with the government is of no value until

sanctioned by parliament, and that we, having the responsibility of carrying it, should have the opportunity of submitting it to the public and parliament at our own time, and in our own way.
I quote from that letter only to show that things have not changed a great deal in the last eighty years. As the French say, "Plus cela change, plus c'est la meme ohose"; and I just suggest to the hon. member for Stan-stead that in these proposals to the provinces we have been at least as frank and open as was that great statesman and leader of the party of which the hon. gentleman is a distinguished member, Sir John Macdonald.
In the course of his speech last evening and today the leader of the opposition raised a number of points with which I should like to deal briefly. First, he made the point that he approves fiscal need grants, but that he would not be prepared to agree to anything which went beyond the requirements of fiscal need. The hon. member for Vancouver East asked what he meant by fiscal need. Of course he did not have an opportunity of replying and I do not suppose the hon. member particularly wished that he should. Well, I have no intention of defining fiscal need, either, but my understanding has always been that a grant to cover fiscal need would be a grant to enable a particular province or particular organization, whatever it might be, to balance its budget, and that no matter how extravagant the administration of the province might be.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext: I would not agree with that definition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Well, that is one suggestion. Another might be that it would1 be a grant or an allocation to a province which would enable that province to maintain an average standard of services without imposing higher than average rates of provincial taxation. But whatever basis one may take, I suppose the broad principle is that the grant or allocation should be sufficient to enable the particular government, provincial or municipal, to discharge its legitimate responsibilities. Later in his speech the leader of the opposition questioned how long we could go on making payments to the less favoured provinces from money collected largely in the two most favoured provinces. Well, I found it hard to understand that position, because it seemed to me that the two attitudes were contradictory. How can you have fiscal need subsidies unless money which is collected in more favourable provinces is spent in less favoured areas? Then he went on to say, as I mentioned a moment ago, that he favoured payments to the extent that they 
met real fiscal need but not to the extent that they exceeded fiscal need; and he contrasted the payments of approximately
840,000,000 under the Sirois proposals with the $226,000,000, roughly, under the 1947 agreements. The first point I wish to make is that that comparison in itself-and I think my hon. friend will agree-is misleading, because the Sirois plan envisaged the assumption by the dominion of servicing provincial debts in addition to fiscal need subsidies. The total outlay for net debt service and sinking fund estimated for 1940 was $73 million. So if you add that to the $40 million contemplated1 by the Sirois report you have something like $120 million.
I think the committee would agree that since 1940 the practical value of taxation fields which are to be turned over to the dominion, or which it was suggested in the Sirois report should be turned over, have been greatly increased. The proposed 1947 agreement was made up of the statutory subsidies plus annual rentals for tax fields now occupied by the provinces.
I believe that on a moment's reflection the committee will agree that the rental for those taxation fields had to be high enough to compensate the so-called more favoured provinces for the tax sources which they were renting, and the rent, of course, is higher than the value of the tax fields in the less favoured provinces. The difference, I suggest to the committee, provides a convenient and, in fact, a largely automatic measure of the economic disadvantage and consequently the fiscal need of the less favoured provinces.
As I listened to the leader of the opposition I thought I should ask him if he considers that British Columbia, for example, is getting a higher rental than the tax fields are worth to that province. Does he believe that the payments to Manitoba and Nova Scotia are in excess of the fiscal needs of those provinces?
Then the leader of the opposition took exception, as did the hon. member for Stan-stead, to the method of making agreements with the provinces individually. Well, I spent some time yesterday evening and I have spent considerable time on other occasions in outlining in some detail the efforts which were made by the dominion government through a series of conferences to arrive at a mutually satisfactory agreement with all the provinces. I see little purpose in my reiterating tonight what I have said on that score.
But I wish to make this observation, that a desire for agreement on both sides is necessary to arrive at an agreement. I do not wish to impute motives to anyone, and indeed I am not doing so, but what has taken place does

Tax Agreements with Provinces
not convince me that there is a genuine desire on the part of all provinces to arrive at agreement. The budget speech of my predecessor in office, the present Minister of Justice, shows what the dominion was willing to offer. Seven of the provinces have now indicated that they are prepared to accept that. Since that budget only a little over a year ago, the governments of two provinces, Quebec and Ontario, have consistently failed to indicate on what terms they would be prepared to confer. It never seemed to me that there was much use in calling a conference without some kind of agenda to work on. Seven provinces have already evinced their desire to enter into an agreement, and there is little to confer on so far as taxing matters are concerned.
I want to repeat what I said before, that the dominion has repeatedly expressed its willingness to confer with all the provinces, and to confer with Ontario and Quebec if they [DOT] would indicate some specific basis for conference.
I know I am not permitted to quote from a previous debate, and I do not intend to do so, but what was said by the Prime Minister as it is reported at pages 69 and 70 as to what Canada did in 1946 and 1947 is exactly what the leader of the opposition recommended in 1941 when he was Premier of Manitoba, namely not to permit one or two provinces to obstruct essential action to give justice to less favoured provinces.
Another point which the leader of the opposition made was that the proposed agreements make for centralization of taxing power. I say the dominion is not asking for the slightest abatement of the constitutional powers of any of the provinces. Their taxing powers remain intact. We are merely seeking to rent-and I use that term, although I know the hon. member for Stanstead took exception to it-taxation fields, which the Sirois report suggested should be exclusively and permanently federal.

That is why I find it so difficult to understand the attitude of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, who was a staunch supporter of the Sirois report. It was the Sirois report which recommended that these powers be exclusively and permanently assigned to the dominion.
I am not going to quote from the speech of the leader of the opposition which was made at the conference of 1941, but I would point out that he strongly endorsed the permanent surrender of income and corporation taxes and succession duties to the dominion.
I do not suggest for one moment that the proposals which we put forward now are the most desirable. We had hoped that, as a result of a general conference, we could arrive at a general over-all understanding. They are perhaps not the best, but certainly in my judgment they are better than nothing at all. And it was no fault of the dominion government, may I say, that we were driven to this particular method.
There are one or two further points. The leader of the opposition referred to the well known statement made by the Prime Minister in 1929 and 1930 to the effect that the raising of money by one government to make grants to be spent by another government was a vicious principle. Neither the Prime Minister nor anybody else has ever disputed the truth of that. But this statement was taken from its context. It referred to unemployment relief grants and to other grants in aid where the provinces had control of expenditures and the' dominion made grants in proportion to the expenditures, the full size of which it could not possibly control.
What is vicious, of course, about such grants is that they are open-ended commitments. The dominion has no possible means of controlling the extent of its liability. But the payments under the present agreements are not grants in aid. They are contractual payments in the form of rents for the use of taxation fields. The rent is determined by an objective and well known formula; the grant does not increase and the province can get no more if its administration is lax or if it is extravagant. I think the principle of a grant is vicious when there is an incentive to extravagance or inefficiency. But that is not true of the payments proposed under this agreement, because if the provinces inflate their budgets they still have to raise money by provincial taxation to balance them.
I believe I have covered most of the points raised. I must say I was not entirely clear, after listening to the leader of the opposition, whether he was for or against these agreements. I gathered, however, that on balance he was for them. He did make one other statement to which I would refer. He said we were backing away from the 1945 proposals. I covered that point yesterday evening in my statement upon introducing the bill. My hon. friend was good enough to quote what I said and, he having quoted it, I wondered how he could justify his stand that we are backing away.

The details of our original proposals may of course change as a result of further study or of developing public opinion or of discussion with provincial governments at a general conference which will be necessary 'before they can be implemented. The proposed contributions which the dominion may be able to make in the field of public investment and social security may, as I have said publicly and as I advised the provinces which were negotiating with us last winter, have to be revised to take into account the substantial increase in the financial payments which the dominion has now undertaken to make as a rental for the tax fields in question.

But the main objectives expressed in those proposals remain the guiding objectives of this government.
I leave it to the sense of the committee to decide whether or not the dominion government is backing away from those proposals.
