[Mr Abbott.]
proceed I want to say that I would have supported the principle of the bill if I had been here when it carried. But that does not mean that I agree with all that has been done.
This afternoon I listened to a couple of speeches which were most interesting, one by the versatile and amiable hon. member for Temiscouata. The hon. member went through quite a lengthy series of legal or mental gymnastics to arrive at a conclusion I would have arrived at through another process, one with which I would agree no matter what process was used. He argued that it was necessary for the dominion and the provincial governments to be independent, but that they should be friendly. I do not think anyone will dispute that conclusion.
Then the hon. member for Stanstead, not quite as versatile, but quite as earnest and a little ponderous, surprised me somewhat with his argument. One of his main arguments was that, while this agreement would be only for five years, it would be difficult to change it at the end of that period and therefore he was opposed to it. He said that it was different from what had happened eighty years ago. After eighty years he now opposes any change whatsoever, and yet in the same breath he says that we would not be able to make a change at the end of five years. I was unable to follow the hon. member in that line of reasoning, but otherwise he was interesting.
One of the things he referred to was that the provinces are responsible for their own position. Speaking for Saskatchewan, I want to say that we would not hesitate to accept that responsibility if all other things were equal. I think I can say the same thing for our sister prairie provinces. In order to do that we would have to turn back the pages of history and start somewhat differently. I shall not take advantage of this opportunity to review the history of Saskatchewan and make a political speech, but I want to remind the committee that it would be possible to do so and make out a good case.
When the dominion government insists upon interfering with the work or the decisions of a provincial government in order to prevent that provincial government from doing something which the dominion feels is within its field, it seems obvious to me that the dominion government has some responsibility. I am going to refer to two things to illustrate what I mean, one having occurred in Alberta and the other in Saskatchewan. I do not sit with the hon. gentlemen of the Social Credit group, so that obviously there are points of disagreement between us, but there is one point of agreement between us. If the people of a province by a democratic election have

Tax Agreements with Provinces
elected a government on a programme which those who sought their votes claimed they could put into effect, then they should be allowed to do it. Whether social credit will work in Alberta we shall never know until it is tried and this government deliberately prevented them from making the experiment. Canada is poorer for not knowing the results of that experience. Having interfered with the democratic decision of the people of Alberta, this government owes that province the necessary fiscal aid to carry out its social services, regardless of what might have been said eighty years ago at the time of confederation.
Recently a new government was elected in Saskatchewan on a somewhat different ticket but through the same democratic process. That government was elected because a majority of the voters felt that their programme was good. One piece of legislation which they passed to carry out their election promises was the farm security act. Because one of the clauses of that act might, through some obscure method of reasoning, be considered to interfere with interest on capital, which this government claims was its exclusive field, the dominion government took steps to see that that particular legislation was disallowed.

I am not asking for ultra vires legislation; I am simply saying that when the dominion government is determined to retain in its possession certain powers, then it must accept certain responsibilities, and one of those responsibilities is to see that the fiscal needs of the province are taken care of. That is the point I am making. I am not going to criticize the government in this debate for what they did-I may do it at some other time, but not today; I am simply 83166-344J
citing this as an illustration of what took place and in order to show that in my belief this government has a responsibility along with these powers.
When the Rowell-Sirois commission presented their report some years ago many of us in Saskatchewan-and this was before the C.C.F. government was elected in that province-felt that there was a great deal of good in that report. I remember going to a meeting at which the former member for my constituency, a supporter of the present administration, gave an exposition of the report to the voters of our city, and I remember being very much interested and listening carefully to his explanation. He indicated complete support for the report at that time. The premier of Saskatchewan at that time was a Liberal, and he also supported the report, as I believe the premier of Manitoba did. Some others did not. But I did not feel the disappointment over these disagreements that many seemed to feel because, When a report on so complex a subject is presented, it is only natural to expect that, until the report has been studied and discussed and mental changes have taken place in consequence, some people will not agree with the report right off the bat. The discussions went on, and finally we had the dominion government's offer to the provinces. Many of us considered that a good thing, and I commend the government for having made those proposals. I think the government deserves commendation for its offer at that time. I go farther and say that the government and the Minister of Finance deserve commendation for the adjustments they have made and for the flexibility of their arrangements in arriving at agreements with the different provinces.
The hon. member for Temiscouata this afternoon said he was sympathetic with the Minister of Finance because of the heavy load he carries. I am not a bit sympathetic with an able man who is well able to carry the load. His bearing of the load will make him an even better man than he is at present, and he is very good. So I waste no sympathy on him because he does not need it. I give him all possible commendation for having been capable of arriving at some kind of solution with seven of the provinces.
But I would point out to the government that Saskatchewan, through its previous and its present administration, indicated its willingness to enter into these taxation agreements, knowing well, from the history of Saskatchewan and considering the way in which we got stuck and our not having industrial organizations which would stand the taxation load which would be required to meet

Tax Agreements with Provinces
the fiscal needs of the province, that we would have to call on the rest of our sister provinces who are more favourably situated in that regard for their contributions. We have the same situation within the province itself because there we have some good areas, some not so good, and some very poor, and we have to ask the good areas to make a larger contribution, so that our social, educational, and welfare services will be better equalized for the men, women and children of the province. We expect the same type of cooperation from our sister provinces. Even though two provinces of this dominion have not yet decided1 to enter into this kind of agreement, we feel that, even at that, we should have had implemented in our province the full amount of the government's original proposals. ' We have not yet got the sixty per cent of the medical, health and welfare proposals of the dominion government. We have not got the full amount of old age pensions and assistance for the employable unemployed assumed by the dominion government, as well as a number of other things. We believe that we should have those things in the province of Saskatchewan.
I want now to say something that is not quite so commendatory of the government. The provinces of Quebec and Ontario through their premiers-I believe that they are called prime ministers down here-have indicated an unwillingness at the present time to enter into this kind of agreement, for reasons of their own, and they are being headlined in the press. Not for one moment am I supporting either one of these gentlemen. I deplore the attitude they are taking, but I do not think they, as only two comers of the triangle, are entirely to blame. While they are being blamed in the press and elsewhere, I feel that the government here has not done all that it might have done to resolve some of these differences and to have brought about a better understanding with these two provinces; and if our situation in Saskatchewan is to depend upon the provinces of Ontario and Quebec entering into agreements with the dominion government I think the dominion government should be infinitely more energetic in trying to bring that about. I do not agree it is the proper attitude for this government to take, to say that what is done for Saskatchewan must depend on Ontario and Quebec entering into an agreement with the dominion government. I think the dominion government should deal with Saskatchewan on the basis of its original proposals, and similarly with any other province willing to enter into an agreement. But if the dominion government will not carry out its original pro-

posals until all the provinces have entered into an agreement, the dominion government should be infinitely more vigorous in trying to bring that about and should carry its share, at least one-third of the blame for these agreements not having been arrived at up to the present time.
(Translation):
Mr. LaCROIX: I had intended to say a few words but owing to the lightning speed with which second reading was proceeded with, I have had no chance to do so.
Here is what I have to say with regard to Bill No. 411, authorizing the government of Canada to enter into agreements with the governments of the provinces, pursuant to which, in return for compensation, the provinces agree to refrain from levying certain taxes for a limited period. May I be permitted to say, at the outset, that while I do not support the stand of the government headed by Mr. Duplessis, who left the conference even before its conclusion, and who has submitted no counterproposal with a view to working out some kind of agreement, I cannot, nevertheless, understand how individual agreements could be entered into with the provinces without the cooperation and outside the presence of the province of Quebec, because in my humble opinion it is contrary to the spirit of the British North America Act that separate agreements should be entered into with the provinces in that respect without the consent of all.
You may tell -me, Mr. Chairman, that in view of the stand taken by Duplessis, no agreement can be reached with Quebec. My answer is that above Duplessis there is the province of Quebec to consider, and that, to my mind, it would have been preferable to enter into no separate agreement with the provinces as long as the possibility of negotiations existed. Indeed, I feel that the economic depression which those agreements are supposed to ward off, will not be prevented if the two richest provinces of this country have no part in them.
It is unthinkable that the province of Quebec, which pays a large part of the taxes, should not be a party to those agreements, from which the western provinces will greatly benefit.	*
I wish you would bear in mind, Mr. Chairman, that I am not discussing the merits of the proposals submitted by the dominion to the Quebec government; I am dealing exclusively with the fact that such separate agreements are likely to undermine the very foundations of confederation and to foster a principle fraught with danger, so that their implement-

Tax Agreements with Provinces
ing may contribute to lead us fM'tiher and farther from our greatest objective, Canadian unity.
I have already had an opportunity to explain in this house what I consider as the reason for the aloofness of Messrs. Duplessis and Drew, and the selfish grounds on which they have taken their stand. I still hold that view, but I deem it my duty to oppose agreements entered into separately with the provincial governments, without Quebec being a party to them.
In concluding, I wish to express the hope that Messrs. Drew and Duplessis may change their stand, because otherwise we shall have a system of double taxation detrimental to all Quebec taxpayers.

I was very much interested, having been connected with the reserve force for a good many years, in what the minister said with reference to reserve training of the army. There were a couple of questions I wished to ask in this connection, and I may say that I am pleased indeed to see that a much larger estimate than usual has been given for this training this year. No one knows the necessity for this better than an officer who has been with the reserve army for a number of years. The question I wish to ask the minister has reference to the training of tank regiments in rural areas, and I speak particularly of the tank regiment in my district. There are a number of squadrons. The regiment is not a city regiment but a rural regiment, and therefore these squadrons are scattered pretty well over two counties.
Some time ago I understood from the commanding officer that it was the intention of the department to send tanks for training purposes to the different squadrons. Perhaps the parliamentary assistant to the minister can tell me whether that is correct.

speakeroldname: Mr. HUGUES LAPOINTE (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is correct.

In criticism of that, it was felt that it was not feasible to send these large tanks, weighing from thirty to forty tons-I have not the exact weight, but that is about what they weigh-over country bridges, rivers and so on. That was not felt to be practicable unless the regiment is brought together in one central place. My suggestion with reference to this particular tank regiment would be that it should be brought to one centre, and if there is to be training with tanks, then it can be done in a more practical way. As a matter of fact, I do not believe tanks could be used in this area if it were attempted to carry out .training by the different squadrons. This is a matter I should like to have the department look into.

I might say also, as the parliamentary assistant knows, that there has been a training centre at the town of Sussex for a good many years. This rural regiment has its headquarters at Hampton, a few miles from Sussex. I would think that the better plan for this regiment and probably for other tank regiments across the country would be to bring them together for a number of days during the year and give them training when they could all be brought together. I should also like to ask the parliamentary assistant if it is the intention to use the camp at Sussex as a training area. Some time ago I heard that training was not to be at Sussex but at Utopia, another camp in the southern part of the province. I might say that Sussex camp has been a training area now for, I think, over fifty years. That area was greatly extended during the war. The parliamentary assistant himself spent some time in Sussex and we were pleased to have him there. I think he knows it is a good training area. I hope consideration will be given to using it as a training area.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for Royal for his constructive remarks. As regards his first point about tank regiments, I think the point he raised has been already appreciated by the department. It is realized that it is quite impossible in some areas where a tank regiment exists, to have training going on in that area. Tanks will be issued to those units in order to permit the men to be trained in the maintenance and operation of those tanks; but I dare say that training as a tank squadron would not take place in areas where it would cause any damage.
As regards Sussex, I regret that I have not the information here. I quite appreciate my hon. friend's point of view. I know of the facilities which exist in Sussex, and were it not for the fact that I should probably be contradicted by other members, I would say that one of the best brigades that ever went overseas was trained in Sussex. However I will look into this matter and give the hon. member the information he seeks.

I have before me a letter from a man who says he joined up in the air force believing that he would be an instrument mechanic; he signed up with that agreement but, after he got in, he was told that there would not likely be a course in that subject and he would just have to take anything at all that was available. He wanted to have a trade of that kind, and there not being a course of that kind in there he said,

Supply-National Defence
"Well, then, can I get out?" He was told, that he could get out, but I understand that in order to do so he has to buy his way out. Is that right?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is quite right.

Will the parliamentary
assistant explain that? How does a man buy his way out?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I have not the regulations before me; but roughly, the principle is that a man who has enlisted for a period of three years, five years, or whatever it may be, and who wishes, for reasons of his own, to withdraw from the service before the expiration of that period, must pay a bounty of so much a month. I believe in the case of the air force, although I would not say for certain, it is S2.50 a month for each month he still has to serve. That provision has always been in the king's regulations. It was there prior to the war and is still in force.

In this case, I would judge that the air force was at fault to some extent, owing to the fact that they took him in believing that he would be an instrument mechanic. Now they are asking him to pay SI00 in order to get out.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: My hon. friend quite realizes that I cannot tell him whether or not the particular air force officers concerned were at fault in this particular case. If he wishes to give me the particulars of the case, I shall be glad to look into it.

I will do that. I will write to the man and then I will speak to the parliamentary assistant.
I have another case. I wish to get a little bit of information in regard to a course. A boy in Peterborough tried to join up at Royal Roads, but his age was just three months out and they would not take him in. But a Royal Canadian Air Force officer was in Peterborough interviewing the different boys, and he said that in 1948 there would be a course there for graduates of high schools with senior matriculation standing, and that they would be graded and given short-term commissions in the Royal Canadian Air Force. Is there to be some special set-up in 1948 for the Royal Canadian Air Force?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The only thing that comes to my mind that would explain this would be that this particular officer would be referring to university training, the equivalent of our Canadian Officers Training Corps in the army or U.N.T.D. in the navy-I do not know exactly what the name for it in the air force is-where a student, having senior matriculation, following the university course can follow the equivalent course in the air force and, after the period of service, be qualified to enter into the air force.

There is another thing I should like to ask in regard to a course or joining up in the Royal Canadian Navy and the Royal Canadian Air Force and the conditions of entry at Royal Roads. Some of the boys in my district or, as I said before, one especially tried to join up and he was just three months over the age. As to age limits, a candidate must have attained the age of sixteen and a half years but not the age of nineteen and a half on July 1 of the year of entry; but in the case of candidates from French classical colleges the maximum age is extended to allow entry up to twenty and a half years on July 1 of the year of entry. These boys feel that they should have the same privilege to join.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The explanation that I could give the hon. member for that is-
I know that has been the rule.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: -that the matter has been looked into, and the authorities in all services looking into the setting up of qualifications necessary to enter these various schools have come to the conclusion that students coming out of these colleges to which my hon. friend was referring would be, generally speaking, one year older than students graduating from high school with 3enior matriculation. In other words, to have two men with equal qualifications coming from two different institutions of the sort, one would, generally speaking, be a year older. In order to permit of a fair representation amongst the students, the regulations were set in that way. This was thoroughly investigated before it was finally decided by the services themselves.

These boys felt that the authorities were haggling over just a few months with respect to their age, and they did not like it. They thought they should have the same privilege.
I have not been able to be present in committee on the defence estimates, owing to meetings of the public accounts committee. Has the minister said anything with regard to bands which are being set up across the country? There is a Major Streeter who is in charge of bands in the army. He is setting up bands, or allowing units to set up military bands and bugle bands across the country. What is the set-up there?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Only bands authorized by headquarters are recognized and receive grants. I can give the hon. member the number of authorized bands and those organized up to date. The principle followed, if I may use that word, is that headquarters decides which units shall be entitled to bands. In the active force I believe two infantry units and one artillery regiment are authorized to have bands. In the reserve units the number is larger, based on the situation that existed before the war. Some units had bands before the war and still have the instruments, so it is only logical that they should be the first to be authorized to have bands now, but nothing final has been done.
Does the department say whether they are to be bugle bands or brass oands?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I believe the request is made by the unit.

Has the parliamentary
issistant any statement on the matter?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am sorry, but all I have here is the number that have been authorized and those already organized.
I do not want to take up the time of the committee. If the parliamentary assistant would just place that information on Hansard I would lie satisfied.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is very short. In the case of the navy, active, four bands are authorized and three have been organized to date. In the case of the navy, reserve, nineteen are authorized and eight have been organized. In the case of the active army eight are authorized and four organized. In the reserve army 317 are authorized, but I have not the figures as to those organized to date. In the air force, active, one is authorized and three are organized; this will have to be readjusted. Each auxiliary squadron is authorized to have a band, but I do not think any have yet been organized.

Some few years ago I asked the then Minister of Munitions and Supply about helicopters. I understand that the United States navy has set up squadrons of these machines, and I wondered if our navy had anything of that sort in mind. They have been a great help in saving lives, in rescuing people who have crashed in planes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I know the air force has a few helicopters at the present time, but I do not know of any plans to develop that further.

The other day I asked the minister several questions to which I hope the 
parliamentary assistant has the answers. I should like to call his attention to one in particular. I asked for a statement of the wastage in the forces, by which I mean a comparative statement of the number taken on strength and the number discharged, say in the most recent six months' period for which the parliamentary assistant may have figures. Then there are other questions I should like answered.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
If the hon. member permits I shall deal first with one of the other questions he asked. I believe he asked if we could give the strength of various units so he might get an idea of the average strength of the reserve forces. I am sorry I did not give him the information yesterday; I had it a few minutes after he asked the question. I have here the strength of three infantry units, two artillery units and two engineer companies. The infantry units are located in Toronto', Windsor, and in British Columbia. In the case of the Toronto unit the strength is 34 officers and 270 other ranks. In British Columbia the regiment has 30 officers and 226 other ranks. The Windsor unit has 32 officers and 262 other ranks. As to artillery, the one field regiment in Ontario has 20 officers and 102 other ranks; the one in Montreal has 28 officers and 278 other ranks. In the case of the engineer companies, one in Quebec has 4 officers and 82 other ranks and one in Ottawa has 6 officers and 40 other ranks. These were given to me because they were the most readily accessible.
With regard to wastage I can give the hon. member the number of discharges over a period of a few months. In April, 1947, there were 746 enlistments and 53 discharges. In March, 1947, there were 568 enlistments and 37 discharges. In February, 1947, there were 700 enlistments and 25 discharges. During the period from October, 1946, to April, 1947, enlistments totalled 12,974 whereas the number of discharges during the same period was 135.
Is that the active force?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is the active force.
Would it be possible to get any figures on the reserve forces?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am afraid I have not those figures.

I should like to make one comment to the parliamentary assistant. The figures for the infantry battalions-and I think on the artillery regiments, though I cannot speak of that from personal knowledge as I am sure the hon. member for Calgary East will be able to do-seem to indicate that

Supply-National Defence
these battalions have not sufficient strength for adequate training. I say that from my own experience. I feel that an infantry battalion with a strength of only 250 including officers is not in a position to train to best advantage. I know the parliamentary assistant will take note of that comment, but I hope he will apply it.

Would the parliamentary
assistant indicate whether or not there are approximate compulsory ages for retirement in all ranks of the permanent force? If there are, what are the ages when, except for special circumstances, it is considered that officers or other ranks should be retired from the permanent force?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I recall giving that
information last year. There are, ages for compulsory retirement of officers, depending upon rank.
Would the parliamentary assistant put that on record?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I would be glad to have that information placed on record, although I have not it at hand.

While that is being looked up, I would bring to the attention of the committee the specific case of an officer who was retired on March 8 of this year. This case was brought to the attention of the hon. member for Yorkton. It refers to an officer who had attained the rank of captain and who was thirty-three years of age at the time of his retirement. This man had made application to be retained in the Canadian forces. He had had eleven years and 233 days of service in the permanent force and the active army, having served overseas, and prior to that had four years and 149 days of service in the nonpermanent active militia, or a total service of about sixteen years.
At this early age of thirty-three years he was anxious to make the army his career. To the best of his knowledge, no adverse reports had been made about him, but he was retired by an officer selection committee under the provisions of K.R. Canada, section 267 (c). Not being compulsorily retired, he received a retiring allowance under part 5 of the Militia Pension Act, amounting to $677.91 per annum.
Mark you, this man had reached only the age of thirty-three years. The pension is to run until he is sixty-five years of age, at which time, if he is still living, he will receive a pension of $1,016.66 per annum. This man worked his way through the ranks of the permanent force and attained the rank of captain. The army has been put to a considerable expense in training him, and the country will now be 83166-345
put to a further expense in providing him with a pension for the rest of his life. In my view he has a considerable number of useful years of service left to him. The country will be placed to the further expense of training someone to take his place. It seems to me that, in respect of a man of only thirty-three years, the Department of National Defence must have strong reasons for retiring him. Otherwise the bases upon which retirements are compulsorily made are unnecessarily wasteful and poor business for Canada.
Yesterday the name of General Worthington was mentioned, a man who has served with considerable distinction in the Canadian permanent force and on the field of battle. General Worthington is not a young man. In the view of the departmental administrative officers, however, he is still able to give excellent service. I would presume that he is in his sixties or thereabouts. Surely a policy under which a man of thirty-three years with the rank of captain can be retired is not in the best interests of Canada. Would the parliamentary assistant comment on this case?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I believe I know the case to which the hon. member refers, because the hon. member for Yorkton brought it to my attention earlier. It is similar to those of many other service personnel who, having served in the permanent force prior to the war and having served in the active service during the war, naturally made progress. Some were commissioned and others received promotions. However, when the time came to establish a peace-time service a choice had to be made among many applicants, and it was found that some were not quite as suitable as others who were applying for appointments to the same rank.
With respect to the matter of pension, it will be recalled that last year we discussed the Militia Pension Act. Provision is made in that act whereby an officer who may have served over a period of years and who has given good service, but who, because of certain factors, suddenly is not found as useful as his subordinates, or others of equal rank, may be retired from the service, with a view to promoting efficiency and economy.
That is exactly what happened in the instance to which the hon. member refers. In view of the fact that this was a relatively young man and the fact that he had1 served eleven years, his case was looked into with even more attention than some others. In addition to the decision rendered by the selection board, assessment was made in his case by serving under officers, in a training

Supply-National Defence

centre. It was on the report made following this period of service that the decision was taken to retire him.
In other words, there is a standardized basis for the assessment of such cases?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Definitely.
It. is not a matter of personal opinion?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Not at all.

And there is something
reasonable and scientific about it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Definitely.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: What particular vicinity does my hon. friend refer to?

That is the point, I do not know. You have an item here of $14,348,000 for the acquisition, construction, purchase, maintenance and so on of national defence properties. I want to be satisfied that the Department of National Defence has not acquired properties in the vicinity of areas where properties have been disposed of to War Assets Corporation. Could the parliamentary assistant give a break-down of this item, giving expenditures in excess of $5,000 or $10,000?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
In connection with the acquisition, construction and purchase of properties, the amounts for the services are as follows:
Navy	 $1,436,940
Army	 5,034,427
Air force	 3,233,200
Most of that was for construction and additions to existing buildings. In the case of the army it would cover the construction of ranges or repairs to such things, and in the case of the navy-I know of one case-it covers the acquisition of property around a magazine in order to create a safety area. I can assure my hon. friend that no buildings are being purchased into which the services are being moved when there are already existing quarters or where facilities have been declared surplus and we now find ourselves under the obligation of purchasing others. During the war some branch of the service may have been in leased quarters, and in order to continue the operation of that station or that division we may find that we cannot lease the property and must acquire some temporary buildings in the meantime.

Would this item cover the
1,000	dwellings which the minister mentioned yesterday were being acquired for the purposes of housing permanent force families?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
This item covers one group of 556 family units and another one of 600 family units, which is more than the minister referred to yesterday.

Supply-National Defence
In those particular housing areas were any military properties declared surplus?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Those are married quarters and none were declared surplus.
I am thinking of buildings which might have been suitable for conversion purposes and which have been declared surplus in those areas.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am informed that in those various areas the services retained all buildings which it was considered might be necessary for conversion into these temporary married quarters.
What are the two areas to which the minister has referred?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: When I referred to two groups I am afraid I gave the wrong impression. There are two separate construction schemes, but they cover many areas, such as Borden, Shilo, Chilliwack, Lachine, Centralia, Calgary, Greenwood, Sea Island, Vancouver, Saskatoon, Valcartier and Suffield.
In none of those areas have buildings which might have been converted been disposed of to War Assets Corporation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There might have been some, but none that were necessary for reconversion.

Clothing and personnel equipment is part of the next item. The officer who reported to the war expenditures committee a year and a half ago indicated to us that the services had ample supplies of clothing and personnel kits to run over varying periods, as I recall it, from three to five years. Would the parliamentary assistant indicate how much it is estimated will be spent under this item this year and also justify to this committee the need for that particular item?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The break-down of clothing and personnel equipment is as follows:
Navy	 $ 682,666
Army	 2,065,878
Air force	 1,600,647

Those seem to be rather large expenditures in view of the large stores which the ordnance officers of the various branches told the war expenditures committee were in reserve. Would the parliamentary assistant elaborate on the need for those expenditures?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
In the case of the active force, army, this item is broken down as follows:
Clothing and necessaries	 $153,000
Officers' clothing	 220,000
Individual equipment	 35,000
Web equipment, trials	 5,000
83166-345J
What is meant by that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: For the testing of various web equipment under certain conditions.
Is it the opinion of the departmental officials that the equipment turned over to War Assets was not suitable for the particular use to which this equipment is being put?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am informed that most of it is completely new equipment. My hon. friend understands that the ordnance service and various other branches of the army are continually making tests of personnel equipment and clothing and that changes are being made from time to time.

There was so much equipment in store that considerable quantities were dumped into the lap of War Assets. Surely conditions have not changed to such an extent in the past year and a half that it is found necessary to buy new equipment. Last evening when there was considerable confusion, in the house just before we adjourned, the minister said, in reply to a question that I had asked, that if I required further information he would give it. I was speaking of the installation for the second time of an asphalt floor in the armoury at Belleville city. It was first installed in 1945 at a cost of approximately $2,800. In the early months of 1947 that floor which had become useless and had failed to fill the bill was torn up and a new floor laid at a cost of nearly $4,500. Information that has come to me is to the effect that the work in the first instance in 1945 was not passed by the inspector. It was in charge of a government official. The return I have received shows that the contractor in that case was paid. It seems to me that something must be wrong with a job which the inspector did not O.K. and which afterwards fell down as he probably thought it would.
Mr.LAPOINTE: Following my hon. friend's remarks last night, I had the file concerning the Belleville armoury brought to me and, after studying it, I find that in 1945 a contract was given to replace the then existing wooden floor by an asphalt floor. At the time the unit that was called upon to use the armoury was an infantry unit, and an asphalt floor was the common thing for infantry units in drill halls. I find from the file that the floor when finished was accepted and certified by the officer, and the contractor was paid, as my hon. friend said. Following that, a changeover was made in the unit and the armoury was put at the disposal of an artillery regiment which used self-propelled equipment, such as tanks use. The use of self-propelled equipment over asphalt flooring had the same effect as it would have on our city streets when tanks are moved around. The floor did not prove adequate for this equipment, and consequently the officer in charge recommended that the floor be taken up and a concrete floor 
be put down, which I understand has been done. The matter is not yet finally decided as far as I can find out from the headquarters file, which I studied this morning.

The officer in charge of the regiment there told me that even when an infantry unit was using the drill hall the dust was so bad that right from the start it affected the men's throats. So it was not much of a job.
Last night I asked the minister as to the possibilities of an armoury being erected in the town of Trenton, and his answer was no. Just on Monday last I was informed by a member of the municipal council of Trenton that certain properties on which they had hoped to erect housing which the municipality is badly in need of and for which plans had been prepared have been taken over by the government, and a government official said, "We are in ahead of you on this. We are going to build an armoury there". That does not agree with the statement made by the minister.

I doubt whether my hon. friend would be willing to accept that as a drill hall. I an) sure he will come back again next year.

I wish to ask the parliamentary assistant a question regarding the control of equipment in camps. At Camp Borden last summer there was a great deal of equipment, and perhaps there is still. One of the men at the camp, without the consent of the commander, took out a motor car and went to Toronto. He was not familiar with the city or the stop signs or the motor by-laws, and yet he was driving along the streets very rapidly. He came to a stop street and ran into some people with whom I am acquainted and smashed up their car, injuring the man and his wife. The department owned that car, but it claimed that this soldier or camp follower had no business taking it out of the camp. He had not consent to take it out and yet he took it out. That would strike me as careless supervision of camp equipment, when any Tom, Dick or Harry could take out motor cars from a camp and
Supply-National Defence

drive to Toronto. I brought the case to the attention of the government and they disclaimed responsibility. Surely citizens have some protection. These quiet people were motoring peaceably along the street when they were run into by this car, which should have stopped but did not. That was an infraction of the city by-laws and yet the department disclaimed responsibility. My question is, has the department responsibility for its equipment? Should not someone be responsible for taking cars or any other equipment-it might have been rifles-away from the camp?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I can only say that there are strict regulations governing the use of army equipment and particularly motor cars. I recall the case to which my hon. friend refers. As I remember, the culprit, if I may use that term, was himself an army driver and, as such, had a certain access to vehicles in this particular camp. Just as my hon. friend's chauffeur when sent out on duty might decade to make a trip on his own account, that is what happened here. The man was authorized to take out the car to do a certain job, and he kept the car instead of returning it, and proceeded to Toronto where he had an accident. He was not on duty. He had a car without orders, without authority. Consequently the department could not be held responsible any more than my hon. friend could be held responsible if his chauffeur had done the same thing; that is, from the purely legal angle. But I can assure my hon. friend that the greatest care is taken to look after service vehicles; and unless there has been a great relaxation, from my own experience during the time I served in the army it was practically impossible to move a vehicle out of anywhere.
Is this man still in. camp?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
No. This particular
man was, I believe, authorized to go out of the camp on duty, but he did not return to camp. He went to Toronto. That is the case to which my hon. friend referred.
Is he still in the camp?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: He was in the camp.
Is he now?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No. Following that, the man was, I believe, .authorized' to go out of friend may know, and was furthermore brought up for discipline, court martialed and found guilty. I think he was eventually discharged from the army.

Just a word further. I want to follow up for a moment the matter which was raised last evening by the hon. member for Wentworth, who made an excel-

lent job of what he said about the sea cadets. I, too, am a bit exercised over just what is to be the future of the sea cadets. Is it going to improve? Are more sea cadets to be trained? Just what is the department going to do for them? As one of the presidents of the Navy League of Canada, Ontario division, for many years, I must compliment the department upon the great assistance it has given to the sea cadet movement all during the war. As a matter of fact, the predecessor of the present minister, now the premier of Nova Scotia, was a warm supporter of the sea cadet corps. Every time he came to Toronto he was given a great reception. During the war the sea cadets did great work. In 1945 I believe there were about 15,000 young men in the ninety-one sea cadet corps in Canada, of whom some 6,000 in thirty-eight corps were in Ontario. I have long taken an active interest in sea cadet corps work because, so far as I can ascertain, not one young man trained in the sea cadet corps was ever in the juvenile court or had anything to do with juvenile delinquency. That is a remarkable tribute to the training these young men get in sea cadet work. What the department does in that regard is highly commendable.
I want to say further that those associated with the work, the men and women who give their time voluntarily, and did so during the war, had a marked influence on the prosecution of the war as far as the navy was concerned, for some 10,000 of the sea cadets during the war served in the navy. I believe about 250 in the merchant marine and perhaps fifty in the air force. I should now like to ask what programme the government has in hand to maintain and assist the development of the whole sea cadet corps programme? At the present time I believe there are some fourteen camps in Canada, more or less.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No.
How many are there?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There are eight now.
The number has been reduced. There were fourteen, though.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There were at one time.

They have now been reduced to eight. Summer camps were effective places for the purpose of getting these young lads off the street and training them. Are the eight camps sufficient to take care of all who are offering themselves for that splendid training?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence

speechtext: I would like to make a suggestion looking to some recognition of the services of such men as David Gibson, who give, not only of their time, but a good deal of financial assistance. Mr. David Gibson of Toronto is dominion president of the Navy League of Canada, and Mr. Gordon C. Leitch of Toronto is president of the Ontario division of it. They and all the men who serve with them give of their time freely. I often wondered if the department had any picture, diploma or certificate which they could send to the headquarters of the navy league-they could hang it in their board rooms-to show the government's appreciation of the services rendered by these men and the officers serving under them during the war.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence

I realize that, especially during the war, everybody who took an active part in the navy league which sponsored these sea cadets did an extraordinary job. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is what one might call the bone of contention. The staff of the army advised that this would be equitable pay for these officers. I believe some of them made representations, and the matter was discussed by the staff and also with university authorities. Following those negotiations, the service set the period of ten days as what they believed to be an equitable period for the service rendered with the C.O.T.C.

I understood that these officers were told before they undertook their work that they would be paid for the full number of days they were actually instructing, based upon the usual manner of calculating those days. Since the parliamentary assistant has not the final information, I shall not press the particular case at the moment further than to say that I feel any reserve army officer who is called upon to perform duties of that kind, or for that matter any duties, should be paid the full amount to which he is entitled, at the ordinary rates, for the period of time he puts in. There should be set no arbitrary period of ten days. If a man did twelve days or fifteen days he should be paid for that number of days, and there should be no attempt

It is quite impossible to get any picture from the estimates as they are now set up as to how the money is being spent. In future years I hope this particular integration will be done away with and that we shall have a picture of all three services presented in the estimates.

where they are going. There is an amount of $14,348,558 for the acquisition, construction, purchase, maintenance and so on of properties. Sundries, including printing and stationery, telephones, teletype, telegrams, postage, office machinery, special training equipment and films, fees for special courses, maintenance grants, miscellaneous services, and other items not included in above, $10,162,195.

On occasions members supporting the government assert that those of us in the opposition do not offer any economic suggestions. Just about a year ago, as reported at page 5058 of Hansard for August, 19, 1946, I said
Several weeks ago the minister said that he would welcome any suggestions that would curtail spending either by the government or by the Department of Rational Defence. I therefore draw his attention to the Canadian inspection board.
On April 1 of this year the United Kingdom and Canada inspection 'board ceased to exist, and from then on it carried on as it does now under the name of the Canadian inspection board. From April 1 to July 1 that inspection board cost this country over $600,000. At that rate it will cost Canada this year over $2,500,-
000.
That establishment was not reduced until March 31 of this year. I readily understand that just because something is drawn to the attention of the government the excess service cannot be wiped out overnight. I say, however, that this represents a gross waste of the taxpayers' money. I know that many of the personnel in the export board did nothing for the six months prior to March 31, 1947. They were on extended leave. They would go to work in the morning, and would be sent home and told to report next day or next week. I know exactly what went on. If there are any other departments which have as little to do as the inspection board had last year, then the sooner they are disbanded or put on a greatly reduced basis, the better.
A return I received a few days ago shows that at present there are 348 civilian personnel on that board. How many of those have had overseas service? However I know that the premises occupied by the inspection board in my own city have been cut down to a point where the inspection board building is now occupied by the Quebec division of the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve.

Shortly after Japan struck in December, 1941, there rose up on the Pacific coast by voluntary effort almost spontaneously a group of auxiliaries who became known as the Pacific Coast Militia Rangers. They were men engaged in the logging industry, in fishing and in farming out in the more remote portions of the coast, and in some cases in the suburbs of the cities and the larger settlements. They did a grand job and they built up a wonderful esprit de corps. The defence department supplied them with certain clothing such as slickers for the rain and hats, also rifles and certain other equipment. The force made a great reputation for itself. After the war, many of the men in the Pacific Coast Militia Rangers wanted to carry on that work and they have been carrying on, I believe, as rifle associations. The present Minister of National Defence when -he visited the coast at Easter of this year announced thalt there was to be a new ranger organiza-

Supply-National Defence
tion formed under the Department of National Defence. I have a dispatch of April 9 in a Vancouver paper, which starts by saying:
Organization of a dominion-wide "people's" defence force made up of trappers, miners, woodsmen and farmers in remote parts of Canada as an addition to the reserve militia was announced here Tuesday by Defence Minister Brooke Claxton at the conclusion of his six-day inspection of west coast defences.
Last night I was amazed to read in the Vancouver Sun, dated July 4, 1947, which came in yesterday, this statement by the chief of staff, Lieutenant-General Charles Foulkes, then visiting in Vancouver. He said:
Formation of a rangers corps to succeed the Pacific Coast Militia Rangers here is being held up only by a technicality which makes it necessary to revise the Militia Act because the force is not a regular army unit.
That report may not be fully accurate. But what is the hitch? We understood from the minister's announcement at Easter that this rangers corps was to be organized under the Department of National Defence. Now apparently for some reason that is not being done. I would point out to the parliamentary assistant that delay in carrying out plans of this type is dangerous. It makes it just that much more difficult to hold the men together, and if the delay is to continue for another year until there can be an amendment to one of the dominion statutes, that is a most discouraging development. I would ask the parliamentary assistant to make a statement tonight in regard to this situation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I know of the organization the minister had in mind when he made that statement on the coast, and that is being planned. The technicality referred to is one which has never before been brought to my attention, and I cannot say whether it exists or not. I have not heard of it before. I quite agree that we should try to go ahead with this organization as quickly as possible. The work which the Pacific Coast Militia Rangers did during the war is well known, and I believe they have affiliated themselves into an association which may be perpetuated through this rangers movement becoming part of the reserve militia. I will look into the point raised by the hon. gentleman.

May I point out to the parliamentary assistant that some of the officials in the department may not be pleased to see this rangers corps established. There is a certain type of military mind that does not like these irregulars. I hope we have none of that kind on the staff at the present time, but they have been known to be at headquarters, and the minister may find that there is somebody
delaying this organization. I would suggest that he personally go into it carefully and see that the rangers are given the proper status without any further delay.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence

There are two points I wish to make. First, I would call the minister's attention to the peculiar situation that exists in connection with the organization grants for what are looked on as newly formed units in the reserve army. I believe the regulations lay down that this grant can be given to any unit which has been more or less just formed since the war as a result of the new reserve army set-up. However, what has happened in a large number of cases is that units which actually are new organizations have been given names belonging to some former unit which they are supposed to perpetuate. For example, in Calgary the 41st anti-tank regiment is claimed to perpetuate the 41st reserve regiment which existed there during the war and is an entirely war-time creation. Actually the only thing it inherited was the name. It did not get men, equipment or anything else. It simply got the name. Nevertheless, owing to the fact that it has the name, it is cut off from receipt of the organization grant. That has caused a certain amount of difficulty, and also misunderstanding on the part of the reserve army unit commanders. I should like to bring this to the minister's attention and ask him, if possible, to have the matter straightened out in a more equitable way than has been done so far, so that units which are in reality new will be able to draw the grant, notwithstanding the fact that they may have inherited a name and nothing else.
The second point I wish to bring up is in connection with the remarks, mentioned yesterday by the hon. member for York West, which were attributed in the Calgary Herald of Thursday, July 3, to General Foulkes when he was out there. He was speaking in connection with C.O.T.C., and he stated, according to the newspaper:
Cadets are being trained as officer instructors capable of forming a nucleus around which a swiftly trained army could be formed in the event of an emergency.

I hope that is not the view of the Department of National Defence, because I do not think the fact that officers are turned out by C.O.T.C. corps now in existence will result in an army being formed much more quickly than we were able to form one on the outbreak of the war in 1939. In other words, we shall have only a certain number more of trained officers, and I certainly hope the Department of National Defence does not think that, owing to the institution of the C.O.T.C. training plan, we shall be able to form an army in a hurry in the event of an emergency. I do not think we shall be able to form it more rapidly than in 1939.
In addition to the fallacy, as I see it, in that statement, which I hope is incorrect, or is an incorrect report, I suggest that statements of that kind react disadvantageously as far as recruitment of the reserve army is concerned. If senior officers of the army, in travelling about the country, make statements of that kind, which are highly publicized, the average young man will say, "What is the use of my joining the reserve army? It is not much needed. These C.O.T.C. boys will have all the jobs as officers to begin with, and there will be no chance of my rising in the organization, because apparently that is all they need when war breaks out. They can get an army in a hurry and there is no use in my putting in training at the present time." It is particularly from that point of view that statements of that kind are harmful, and I hope this one was incorrect. Can the minister comment on those two matters?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member would not disagree with the view, which has been so repeatedly expressed, that it is a good thing to have a very large number, as far as we can, of well trained officers.
I am very much in favour of it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Everyone is agreed on that. On the other hand, in the event of war there will always be room for others; but in between we hope we shall be able to develop practices whereby promising men having qualities of leadership, education and physique will be given every possible chance of encouragement to qualify as officers. We hope our kind of force-and I mean by force the force of the three services-will be one which will give opportunity for a career for young and promising men either in the active or in the reserve forces.
With regard to the other question raised, the amount provided for grants to units is $375,308, and provision is made for the kind

of allowance to which the hon. gentleman has referred. I think that is amply taken care of.
Do I understand the minister to say that he will look into the matter of organization grants and have that difficulty straightened out?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The weapons in question were 25-pounder guns which had been manufactured at Sorel Industries and the modifications of which were gradually applied and are still being applied in the armament depots of Canada. These modifications cost a good deal. It would have been much easier to have made the gun with the modifications than to have made the gun, and added the modifications later. It is an expensive proposition, but the modifications were proven to be necessary in consequence of war-time experience. They were necessary in order to bring the weapons up to date. They are the most up-to-date weapons and therefore we feel the expense was justified.

The minister is aware, I believe, that I know a little about guns, and I should like him to tell us when these guns were completed, lacking in all these modifications. At the end of the war, our guns, many of which were made in 1942 and 1943, carried
if I remember correctly, about twenty-seven modifications. Most of these modifications had been put on by our own men in our own unit workshops, and those that had not, had been done in the ordinary army ordnance workshops. When were these guns completed and delivered to the army, and what are the modifications that would run to $2,000 apiece? Unless you practically rebuild the gun I cannot see why it should require that amount of money.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I believe the hon. member knows enough about guns and the cost of them to realize that $2,000 does not represent a very large proportion of the cost of a gun. In this case, production was begun, I believe, in 1941 or 1942, and modifications came in from time to time. Then they accumulated, and my colleague the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply was face to face with the problem of production. There is always the question whether you produce with modifications or without, and whether you take the time to produce the modifications or not. I think he was faced with that problem almost from the outset of the war until the end. Almost the greatest delays in the production of war materials, after you get the initial plans, I should think he would agree, were the modifications made in them. Frequently the modifications cost a good deal more than the original weapon. In the case of the 25-pounder gun, we began production in 1941 or 1942. Modifications began at once. Some of them were made in some weapons and some were not. They have gone up, I think, to something of the magnitude of twenty-five or thirty modifications. I have seen armament depots across Canada where there are still many modifications. They are always being made.
But were those guns never delivered?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is right. Some of the guns were delivered and used in Europe, and brought back. Others were never delivered. We have both. As an illustration of this, I might mention the Mosquito aeroplanes. Throughout the length of the war I think there were some eighteen modifications which accumulated. To make the eighteen modifications with respect to each Mosquito would cost $15,000 today.

This item deals with research. I think it is one of the most important items in the defence estimates, because quite often in the past we have blamed- our defence on the basis of the last- war we fought, instead, of looking ahead to the one which might occur in the future. I do not think our own military men were any worse ini this respect than- the military authorities of any

other country. I believe, however, that we have learned a great deal from the last war with regard to the importance of research. The minister should give us some idea of how our research is being carried on. Is it being carried on in conjunction with, the universities in Canada? Are they given certain problems to solve for the department? Is it being carried on through our national research council? What coordination is there between civilian and national defence research? In all research work, when men are seeking the solution of a certain problem, they quite often stumble on other things which are of value but which may not be of any value to them. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
In response to the interest expressed by the hon. member for Melfort, I am indeed glad to make a brief statement on the subject of defence research. The Department of National Defence Act was amended on April 1 of this year to provide for the establishment of a defence research board as a permanent part of the department. The board consists of five ex officio and six appointed members serving under a full-time chairman, Doctor O. M. Solandt. The ex officio members are the chiefs of staff of the three armed forces, the president of the national research council and the deputy minister of national defence. The appointed members are Professor C. H. Best of the university of Toronto; Professor Paul Gagnon of Laval university; Colonel R. D. Harkness of the Northern Electric Company; Professor J. H. L. Johnstone of Dalhousie university; Professor Otto Maass of McGill university and Professor G. M. Shrum of the university of British Columbia. The country is most fortunate in obtaining the advice and guidance of such a distinguished group. Each one of them is not only an outstanding leader in his own field, but has also made an important contribution to the defence of Canada in the past war.
LTnder the guidance of this board, good progress has been made in setting up a permanent organization for defence research. This organization is already beginning to take its place as an essential part of the defence of Canada. It can be regarded as a fourth service, and there is every reason to believe that it will play an increasingly important part in military affairs in the future.
The organization under the defence research board will consist of a headquarters staff, advisory committees and a few research establishments. The ultimate aim of the whole organization will be to make available to the armed forces of Canada all the scientific resources of Canada and of other countries. The headquarters staff will be the main link with the armed forces, getting from them their research requirements and conveying to them the latest results of scientific research. The advisory committees will serve to make available to the armed forces the best scientific advice that is available in Canadian government, university and industrial research laboratories. They will also help to keep the whole scientific community of the country in touch with the problems of defence to facilitate rapid mobilization in time of need. In order to avoid any unnecessary duplication of research facilities, the research stations of the board will deal only with those problems of the armed forces which have little or no civilian interest. In other fields, such as electronics and aeronautics, it will make use of existing research laboratories, especially those of the national research council. In all its work, the board will give priority to problems in which Canada, has some special interests for which our facilities are specially suited. Experience has already shown that well-directed defence research produces many results that are of considerable direct and indirect value to the civilian economy.
In planning this organization, the government has had clearly in mind the vital need for continuity in research. This new organization is no mere temporary addition to our armed forces. It is a fully integrated part, of the defences of the country. It must be staffed and equipped, to take a long term view of the scientific requirements of defence, and it must continue in being as long as there is a need for defence forces. Further, to ensure that research receives adequate consideration of the highest level, the director general of defence research has been given the status of a chief of staff, is a member of the chiefs of staff committee and defence council and attends meetings of the defence committee of the cabinet.
Coordination with civilian research and industry is effected through a number of committees. I can assure the hon. member that the important problem to which he has directed attention is being given the utmost consideration, and that the organization is already in being to deal with it in a way which I am sure he would approve.

I am certainly pleased that the minister has made this statement, and particularly pleased that there is cooperation with industry and our educational institutions in this respect.

I should like to take only a few moments to bring to the attention of the committee what I consider is still an important problem, namely that of immigration. I shall not weary the committee tonight with the old arguments which have been used on many occasions before; nor am I going to reiterate the various arguments which are being used in the senate chamber, in the various forums in Canada and in the service clubs.
I am not going to discuss principles tonight, either, not because I believe the principle is not important, but I am convinced that not only are the principles of immigration understood in Canada, but they are accepted throughout the country. What I am concerned about is the matter of administration. I consider it important that the principles we accept should be translated into action. As things stand, we are not doing enough. It is true that over the period of months governments have evolved a policy which is commendable, but at the same time it is not bringing about results. Perhaps that is inevitable where we have a day-to-day policy, and particularly when we realize that the Department of Mines and Resources is a large one and has in it many important agencies.
The blue book indicates that in that department matters pertaining to the Northwest Territories are placed. Indian affairs form part of it, as does the dominion observatory. Indeed the department covers some thirty boards, branches and bureaux. I have nothing but praise for the department in the manner in which it has carried out its various diversified functions, but I think it is impossible under the present arrangement, to do justice to vital problems such as immigration. The first thing we must do is to let the immigration branch stand on its own feet. During the period of great immigration to this country, and in the days of our greatest prosperity the department of colonization and immigration dealt with some 2,835,000 people from 1901 to 1913. When the flow dwindled the department contracted, and was tucked away in the Department of Mines and Resources where it has remained ever since. It is an efficient department, but at the same time entirely circumscribed.
Today's papers indicate that the committee on Indian affairs has asked for the setting up of a separate Indian affairs department. I notice by the press that Senator Crerar, a former minister of mines and resources, is quoted to have said that Canada's natural resources have been neglected to a point
that was almost tragic. I think the time has come to put the immigration department on a full-time basis, to reconstitute a separate department. If the government does not see fit to do that, then the least it can do is to appoint a deputy minister of immigration. The Department of National Revenue has two deputies; the Department of National Health and Welfare has two deputies, and the Department of National Defence has one deputy with three associate deputies.
The Northwest Territories in themselves have unlimited horizons, and that in itself provides an inspiring job. There is an empire there which needs developing, and that will take all the energies of a full-time deputy minister. The Indian affairs committee suggested that the department should be unscrambled by having a deputy devote his entire time to Indian affairs. I know it is a bold step, in these days when we hear so much of bureaucrac}q to suggest a further enlargement. That sort of thing is looked upon with some disfavour, but I would recall to hon. members that, during the war and its aftermath, when important problems came to the front we did not hesitate to set up departments of government which were answerable to this house. For instance, there were the Department of Munitions and Supply and the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, both created to meet pressing needs. When the need had passed, one department was closed down and the minister has told us that some day the department of reconstruction and supply will go out of existence.
Immigration today and for the immediate future constitutes a problem of national significance. It offers a challenge which we must meet boldly. If we temporize; if we allow it to bog down administratively, we are likely not to reap great benefits. Another aspect of immigration is the regulations. Anyone who has made any study of the regulations will realize that to some extent they are hot logical. If a nephew is twenty-one years of age, he is admissible under the regulations; if he is over twenty-one years of age, he is not admissible. I could never understand what difference it makes. If a man is in good health, is able to work and has someone here in Canada willing to assume responsibility, what earthly difference does it make whether he is twenty-one or twenty-two years of age, so long as he fits into our economy? I can see where in years to come we shall have a lot of people making affidavits before the old age pensions board to the effect that they are really a little older than they are supposed to be.
