I do not like the category method of selection because it smacks too much of the United States system. Like the United States system, it is meant to keep people out, not to let them in. We should admit to Canada anyone who meets our requirements and can conform to our standards. We need hundreds of thousands of people. If the prospective immigrant has a relative here, no matter of what degree, so much the better. If he has not a relative but has a friend who is willing to undertake that he will not become a public charge, then that ought to be good enough.
We have been told that transportation is a difficulty, but recently the premier of Ontario showed us one way of cutting through red tape. The country was much impressed by the action he took in going over to England and arranging for plane transportation for a great number of people. Even today he has two ministers of his government in England arranging various details. I have here a clipping from the Globe and Mail of July 9, datelined London, which reads:
More than 600,000 Britons have made definite plans to migrate, according to the figures given in a man-power survey made by Political and Economic Planning, an independent research organization, and published here today.
We need that kind of people and we ought to make a serious bid for them. If the providing of passage is necessary to lure them to this country, then we ought to make sure that ships are available. I can recall when there was nothing we could do about transportation, but immediately after the premier of Ontario was able to make arrangements to fly people here, we were able to arrange for a ship. It seemed to come out of the thin air, but it will carry some 600 passengers a month. I think we now have transportation for almost 3,000 a month.
Some time ago we were happy to hear the minister announce that 5,000 persons from the displaced persons camps would be admitted to Canada at once. Newspaper reports indicate that the quota has been filled completely, although the people are not yet here. One question one must ask is: What now? From what we know as members, from the letters we get and from the people we see, we know that the surface has not even been scratched so far as people who have someone in Canada willing and able to stand good for them are concerned.
At the present time Britain is admitting 4,000 immigrants a week and has already admitted some 500,000 into that country. This is an urgent problem. We cannot afford to delay. We cannot afford to wait for the international refugee organization, because it may never

function, From all indications the British are looking after their own zone; the French are looking after their zone, and the United States are looking after theirs. We in Canada must face the facts. We have pledged ourselves to provide a home for a fair share of Europe's refugee population who have roots in this country, not only of kinship, but of general national origin. This means that sooner or later we shall take a certain number. With our population, our resources and our absorptive capacity, my suggestion is that we do not wait too long. We ought to begin now to admit those who will eventually come here in any event, because delay is causing incalculable harm at the moment. To bring them over now would be, not only in their own best interests, but in our best interests, for other countries are making very much of the opportunities and are taking off the most skilled, the farmers, and the technicians in every calling, and if we delay we shall find ourselves with only the second best. I think it is time for us to make big plans and to make them at once.
One thing we have to be sure of is that no one shall come into this country without the approval of the government. I think we are all agreed that there is no room for private enterprise in that field.
In view of the statement made recently by the deputy minister that the quota of
5.000	has been used up, it is time that a new declaration should be made. The piecemeal attempt that we are making now is not finding complete favour with the Canadian people. The time has come when we must stop nibbling at this problem and take a good bite at it. Actually we can digest more than we think we can. On this particular question I feel that the people in the country generally are ahead of the government. They are not only willing but anxious that people should be brought in, and my suggestion is that the government make a bold declaration of policy. This constant business of allowing a certain number in today and another number tomorrow leaves us in an uncertain position, and for that reason, rather than the government making declarations from time to time, I suggest that they boldly declare now that we shall allow in a certain number, be it 20,000,
30.000	or 50,000 so that not only can we in Canada plan, but the people who are charged with this responsibility can also plan in order that we may get these people over here as quickly and as surely as possible, not only, as I said, in their own best interests, but in our own best interests too.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Acting Minister of Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I should like to cor-

Supply Mines and Ressources
rect one or two statements that have been made by the hon. member. The first one I think it is important to correct because it was made not only by the hon. member but on the radio tonight and it has also been made in the press. It was that the committee on Indian affairs recommended that Indian affairs be a separate department of government. As a matter of fact that was not the recommendation. The recommendation was that all Indian affairs be in one department, and as I understand it, be in the present department. My hon. friend knows there was a separation of the department a year ago, and the committee recommends that Indian affairs be now reunited in one department.
I should also like to correct the hon. member's impression as to immigration. In his remarks he gave the impression that a quota of 5,000 immigrants had been established by the government. That is not the case. There are three types of immigration: first, immigration from the United Kingdom and from the United States-British and United States immigration; that is unlimited. Any man who is able to get to Canada from Britain or the United States and who has good health and sufficient funds to establish himself here is entitled to come, without limit.
Then there is the ordinary immigration from some non-enemy countries, which again is practically unlimited-immigration such as the Dutch settlers, some of whom arrived recently.
The 5,000 figure had to do wholly with men and women in displaced persons camps. Arrangements have been made with respect to these, and authority was given to bring in
5,000.	These 5,000 have now been selected, and today the governor in council authorized a second 5,000. That is merely to coordinate the work of those engaged in selecting displaced persons and in placing them in Canada in order that one part of the organization may not get out of step with the other.
Are they all coming from continental Europe?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: They are coming from displaced persons camps, which are all in Europe.
There are no limitations on those who may come from the United Kingdom?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
No limitations at all. There is nothing to stop any British subject resident in the United Kingdom from coming to Canada if he can get transportation and if he has good health and funds sufficient to establish himself. I simply make these few remarks now, which I shall extend at the next sitting, because I do not want the impression left
that Canada is carrying on a limited immigration policy. We have an active immigration policy. The facilities for carrying on immigration are being improved each month, and we look for very satisfactory results by the year's end.

What provision is there that a person in the United Kingdom with a certain amount of money will be able to bring his money to establish himself in Canada? Is he allowed to bring a certain number of pounds?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
That is a matter wholly between the resident of the United Kingdom and his government. The United Kingdom has exchange control, as has Canada. The amount that the British treasury will permit a British immigrant to bring to Canada is a matter that depends on the circumstances and depends on the viewpoint of the treasury in the particular case.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
